📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The longest-running climate talks in history came to a disappointing conclusion on Sunday as negotiators failed to come to an agreement on a shared political direction on climate change.
  • After two days of extended talks, representatives from country after country, tiredness etched into each face, voiced their opposition to the so-called "Antalya Pact.".
  • Sources indicate that "I understand that there is no agreement on this text.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The longest-running climate talks in history came to a disappointing conclusion on Sunday as negotiators failed to come to an agreement on a shared political direction on climate change.

After two days of extended talks, representatives from country after country, tiredness etched into each face, voiced their opposition to the so-called "Antalya Pact.".

Sources indicate that "I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted," remarked Murat Kurum, Turkish president of the COP31 climate summit.

One of the main sticking points: the words "fossil fuels." While some nations, including petrostates like Saudi Arabia and Russia, wanted them omitted from the text, others saw it as a "step backwards" not to include them.

Around 130 parties — among them vulnerable island nations, developing countries and richer EU members — called for the reintroduction of the two words into the text, to no avail. And so many refused to support the adoption of the final COP agreement.

The deadlock signals a failure for the UN process. But the number of countries willing to walk away from what they saw as a weak text was, arguably, a show of strength, and one that had been long coming.

The phrase "fossil fuels" first appeared three years ago in the closing decision of COP28 in Dubai with the promise of "transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems, in just, orderly and equitable manner." But it has been omitted from every text since.

Yet this year's climate summit was the first to acknowledge that the world will breach the critical 1.5-degree Celsius (2.7-degree Fahrenheit) threshold that scientists said would safeguard the world from the worst impacts of planetary heating.

It has been revealed that and so, the pressure was on for progress; to turn pledges from previous years into concrete action. But that progress didn't come.

"We don't celebrate the deep divisions exposed or the lack of a political signal from COP31 capable of driving climate action in line with science, equity and the law," said Nikki Reisch, director of the climate and energy program at the Center for International Environmental Law.

"But the rejected text would have done more harm than good.".

The lack of agreement was not solely about fossil fuels; money also played a part.

Developing nations have long argued that they need additional financing, both as a means for them to move away from coal, oil and gas, but also to help them cope with the consequences of rising temperatures.

Sources indicate that countries all over the world are being battered by extreme weather events. Catastrophes like flooding, drought and wildfires have been fueled and worsened by rising global temperatures. Often the worst hit are poorer countries with low rates of greenhouse gas emissions.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

According to recent reports, and yet, richer states behind much of the historical emissions are increasingly unwilling to foot the bill. Dissatisfaction at home due to higher food and fuel prices has left many governments loathe to pay more to finance climate action abroad.

With the United States  — the world's biggest historical emitter  — now absent from negotiations and on the verge of leaving the United Nation's Framework Convention on Climate Change, the European Union was portrayed as this year's villain with some observers accusing the EU of hypocrisy.

"You can't demand action and then block the finance that makes this possible," Fanny Petitbon, policy analyst at 350.org, mentioned in a statement.

As the world's largest provider of climate finance, the EU reportedly refused to negotiate on providing additional finance and has repeatedly called for other nations to step up.

The failure to find an agreement is a particularly bitter turn of events for countries that face ever worsening impacts of climate change, like the island states that are being confronted by a reality that could see their countries wiped off the map as sea levels rise.

Although the Turkey-led electrification agenda calling for an increase in global electricity consumption to 35% by 2035 was not formally adopted — it made up part of the rejected final agreement — more than 90 countries pledged to move forward regardless.

Industry observers note that it's not a silver bullet. There was no agreement on ensuring the increase was forged only through clean, renewable energy. But it would still signal forward momentum, driven by economic forces and a need for home-grown energy security.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Industry observers note that and there are other hopes. The second conference on the Just Transition Away from Fossil Fuels will take place in Tuvalu in July 2027. Initiated at the COP30 conference last year in Belem, Brazil, it has seen increasing support from countries putting together concrete roadmaps for abandoning coal, oil and gas.

Recent findings suggest that there has been much talk of blame and who is responsible for the breakdown and collapse of talks. What is clear is that the UN climate summits need reform. Progress, when it does happen, is slow. The present model, based on consensus, requires all countries to agree on every measure. There have been many calls for majority-rule decision making, which might have forced the inclusion of language like "fossil fuels" into the text.

But ultimately, this is not the time to focus on fault. As the climate crisis accelerates, governments need to reflect — and swiftly — on what can be done outside of these UN processes, within their nations, to speed up climate action.

"The take-home message from COP31 is clear: the world must do much more to confront the climate crisis — and it must do it now," said UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres in a statement.

#127921. Hundreds of millions at risk from Chinese shopping app malware

📅 02 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1929 w)

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

Hundreds of millions at risk from Chinese shopping app malware

📅 02 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1929 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It is one of China’s most popular shopping apps, selling clothing, groceries and just about everything else under the sun to more than 750 million users a month.
  • But according to cybersecurity researchers, it can also bypass users’ cell phone security to monitor activities on other apps, check notifications, read private messages and change settings.
  • While many apps collect vast troves of user data, sometimes without explicit consent, experts say e-commerce giant Pinduoduo has taken violations of privacy and data security to the next level.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is one of China’s most popular shopping apps, selling clothing, groceries and just about everything else under the sun to more than 750 million users a month.

But according to cybersecurity researchers, it can also bypass users’ cell phone security to monitor activities on other apps, check notifications, read private messages and change settings.

And once installed, it’s tough to remove.

While many apps collect vast troves of user data, sometimes without explicit consent, experts say e-commerce giant Pinduoduo has taken violations of privacy and data security to the next level.

In a detailed investigation, CNN spoke to half a dozen cybersecurity teams from Asia, Europe and the United States — as well as multiple former and current Pinduoduo employees — after receiving a tipoff.

Industry observers note that multiple experts identified the presence of malware on the Pinduoduo app that exploited vulnerabilities in Android operating systems. Company insiders said the exploits were utilized to spy on people and competitors, allegedly to boost sales.

“We haven’t seen a mainstream app like this trying to escalate their privileges to gain access to things that they’re not supposed to gain access to,” stated Mikko Hyppönen, chief research officer at WithSecure, a Finnish cybersecurity firm.

“This is highly unusual, and it is pretty damning for Pinduoduo.”.

Malware, short for malicious software, refers to any software developed to steal data or interfere with computer systems and mobile devices.

Evidence of sophisticated malware in the Pinduoduo app comes amid intense scrutiny of Chinese-developed apps like TikTok over concerns about data security.

Some American lawmakers are pushing for a national ban on the popular short-video app, whose CEO Shou Chew was grilled by Congress for five hours last week about its relations with the Chinese government.

The revelations are also likely to draw more attention to Pinduoduo’s international sister app, Temu, which is topping US download charts and fast expanding in other Western markets. Both are owned by Nasdaq-listed PDD, a multinational tech giant with roots in China.

While Temu has not been implicated, Pinduoduo’s alleged actions risk casting a shadow over its sister app’s global expansion.

Sources indicate that there is no evidence that Pinduoduo has handed data to the Chinese government. But as Beijing enjoys significant leverage over businesses under its jurisdiction, there are concerns from US lawmakers that any company operating in China could be forced to cooperate with a broad range of security activities.

The findings follow Google’s suspension of Pinduoduo from its Play Store in March, citing malware identified in versions of the app.

An ensuing report from Bloomberg said a Russian cybersecurity firm had also identified potential malware in the app.

Pinduoduo has previously rejected “the speculation and accusation that Pinduoduo app is malicious.”.

CNN has contacted PDD multiple times over email and phone for comment, but has not received a response.

Pinduoduo, which boasts a user base that accounts for three quarters of China’s online population and a market value three times that of eBay (EBAY), wasn’t always an online shopping behemoth.

Founded in 2015 in Shanghai by Colin Huang, a former Google employee, the startup was fighting to establish itself in a market long dominated by e-commerce stalwarts Alibaba (BABA) and JD.com (JD).

It succeeded by offering steep discounts on friends-and-family group buying orders and focusing on lower-income rural areas.

It has been revealed that pinduoduo posted triple digit growth in monthly owners until the end of 2018, the year it listed in Upcoming York. By the middle of 2020, though, the increase in monthly users had slowed to around 50% and would continue to decline, according to its earnings reports.

It was in 2020, according to a current Pinduoduo employee, that the firm set up a team of about 100 engineers and product managers to dig for vulnerabilities in Android phones, develop ways to exploit them — and turn that into profit.

According to the source, who requested anonymity for fear of reprisals, the company only targeted users in rural areas and smaller towns initially, while avoiding users in megacities such as Beijing and Shanghai.

“The goal was to reduce the risk of being exposed,” they noted.

By collecting expansive data on user activities, the manufacturer was able to create a comprehensive portrait of users’ habits, interests and preferences, according to the source.

This allowed it to improve its machine learning model to offer more personalized push notifications and ads, attracting customers to open the app and place orders, they said.

The team was disbanded in early March, the source added, after questions about their activities came to light.

PDD didn’t reply to CNN’s repeated requests for comment on the team.

Approached by CNN, researchers from Tel Aviv-based cyber firm Check Point Research, Delaware-based app security startup Oversecured and Hyppönen’s WithSecure conducted independent analysis of the 6.49.0 version of the app, released on Chinese app stores in late February.

According to recent reports, google Play is not available in China, and Android owners in the country download their apps from local stores. In March, when Google suspended Pinduoduo, it noted it had found malware in off-Play versions of the app.

The researchers found code designed to achieve “privilege escalation”: a type of cyberattack that exploits a vulnerable operating system to gain a higher level of access to data than it’s supposed to have, according to experts.

“Our team has reverse engineered that code and we can confirm that it tries to escalate rights, tries to gain access to things normal apps wouldn’t be able to do on Android phones,” said Hyppönen.

The app was able to continue running in the background and prevent itself from being uninstalled, which allowed it to boost its monthly active user rates, Hyppönen stated. It also had the ability to spy on competitors by tracking activity on other shopping apps and getting information from them, he added.

Check Point Research additionally identified ways in which the app was able to evade scrutiny.

The app deployed a method that allowed it to push updates without an app store review process meant to detect malicious applications, the researchers said.

They also identified in some plug-ins the intent to obscure potentially malicious components by hiding them under legitimate file names, such as Google’s.

“Such a technique is widely used by malware developers that inject malicious code into applications that have legitimate functionality,” they said.

Sources indicate that in China, about three quarters of smartphone users are on the Android system. Apple (AAPL)’s iPhone has 25% market share, according to Daniel Ives of Wedbush Securities.

Sergey Toshin, the founder of Oversecured, said Pinduoduo’s malware specifically targeted different Android-based operating systems, including those used by Samsung, Huawei, Xiaomi and Oppo.

CNN has reached out to these companies for comment.

Toshin described Pinduoduo as “the most dangerous malware” ever found among mainstream apps.

Sources indicate that “I’ve never seen anything like this before. It’s like, super expansive,” he said.

Most phone manufacturers globally customize the core Android software, the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), to add unique features and applications to their own devices.

Recent findings suggest that toshin found Pinduoduo to have exploited about 50 Android system vulnerabilities. Most of the exploits were tailor made for customized parts known as the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) code, which tends to be audited less often than AOSP and is therefore more prone to vulnerabilities, he said.

Pinduoduo also exploited a number of AOSP vulnerabilities, including one which was flagged by Toshin to Google in February 2022. Google fixed the bug this March, he mentioned.

According to Toshin, the exploits allowed Pinduoduo access to users’ locations, contacts, calendars, notifications and photo albums without their consent. They were also able to change system settings and access users’ social network accounts and chats, he remarked.

It has been revealed that of the six teams CNN spoke to for this story, three did not conduct full examinations. But their primary reviews revealed that Pinduoduo asked for a large number of permissions beyond the normal functions of a shopping app.

They included “potentially invasive permissions” such as “set wallpaper” and “download without notification,” said René Mayrhofer, head of the Institute of Networks and Security at the Johannes Kepler University Linz in Austria.

Suspicions about malware in Pinduoduo’s app were first raised in late February in a report by a Chinese cybersecurity firm called Dark Navy. Even though the analysis didn’t directly name the shopping giant, the report spread rapidly among other researchers, who did name the tech giant. Some of the analysts followed up with their own reports confirming the original findings.

Soon after, on March 5, Pinduoduo issued a upcoming update of its app, version 6.50.0, which removed the exploits, according to two experts who CNN spoke to.

Two days after the patch, Pinduoduo disbanded the team of engineers and product managers who had developed the exploits, according to the Pinduoduo source.

According to recent reports, the next day, team members found themselves locked out of Pinduoduo’s bespoke workplace communication app, Knock, and lost access to files on the company’s internal network. Engineers also found their access to major data, data sheets and the log system revoked, the source mentioned.

It has been revealed that most of the team were transferred to work at Temu. They were assigned to different departments at the subsidiary, with some working on marketing or developing push notifications, according to the source.

A core group of about 20 cybersecurity engineers who specialize in finding and exploiting vulnerabilities remain at Pinduoduo, they remarked.

Toshin of Oversecured, who looked into the enhancement, remarked although the exploits were removed, the underlying code was still there and could be reactivated to carry out attacks.

Pinduoduo has been able to grow its user base against a backdrop of the Chinese government’s regulatory clampdown on Substantial Tech that began in late 2020.

That year, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology launched a sweeping crackdown on apps that illegally collect and use personal data.

In 2021, Beijing passed its first comprehensive data privacy legislation.

The Personal Information Protection Law stipulates that no party should illegally collect, process or transmit personal information. They’re also banned from exploiting internet-related security vulnerabilities or engaging in actions that endanger cybersecurity.

Pinduoduo’s apparent malware would be a violation of those laws, tech policy experts say, and should have been detected by the regulator.

“This would be embarrassing for the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, because this is their job,” said Kendra Schaefer, a tech policy expert at Trivium China, a consultancy. “They’re supposed to check Pinduoduo, and the fact that they didn’t find (anything) is embarrassing for the regulator.”.

The ministry has regularly published lists to name and shame apps found to have undermined user privacy or other rights. It also publishes a separate list of apps that are removed from app stores for failing to comply with regulations.

Pinduoduo did not appear on any of the lists.

CNN has reached out to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the Cyberspace Administration of China for comment.

On Chinese social media, some cybersecurity experts questioned why regulators haven’t taken any action.

Recent findings suggest that “Probably none of our regulators can understand coding and programming, nor do they understand technology. You can’t even understand the malicious code when it’s shoved right in front of your face,” a cybersecurity expert with 1.8 million followers wrote last week in a viral post on Weibo, a Twitter-like platform.

The post was censored the next day.

CNN’s Kristie Lu Stout and Sean Lyngaas contributed reporting.

#127920. Industry News: Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1556 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1556 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A upcoming approach to weight loss could help the body burn more fat while preserving muscle, potentially overcoming one of the major drawbacks of existing obesity treatments.
  • It has been revealed that in experiments with mice, the compound improved blood sugar regulation, reduced harmful blood fats, and helped obese animals lose fat without a significant reduction in lean muscle mass.
  • According to recent reports, the findings, published in Science Advances, suggest a promising upcoming direction for treating obesity, diabetes, and fatty liver disease.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A upcoming approach to weight loss could help the body burn more fat while preserving muscle, potentially overcoming one of the major drawbacks of existing obesity treatments. Researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, have identified a compound that increases the amount of energy the body uses rather than simply reducing how much food a person eats.

It has been revealed that in experiments with mice, the compound improved blood sugar regulation, reduced harmful blood fats, and helped obese animals lose fat without a significant reduction in lean muscle mass. It also increased energy expenditure by up to 18%, even though the mice did not become more physically active or experience an increase in body temperature.

According to recent reports, the findings, published in Science Advances, suggest a promising upcoming direction for treating obesity, diabetes, and fatty liver disease. The experimental compound also appeared to enhance the benefits of popular weight-loss medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy when the treatments were used together. However, its effectiveness and safety have not yet been established in humans.

A Different Approach to Weight Loss Than Ozempic.

Recent findings suggest that over the past five years, medications known as GLP-1 drugs have transformed the treatment of obesity and other metabolic conditions, including diabetes and fatty liver disease. Drugs marketed as Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, and Zepbound have helped many patients achieve substantial weight loss while improving their ability to regulate blood sugar.

Despite these benefits, the medications have key limitations. Nausea and other digestive problems can make treatment difficult for some patients. Because these drugs reduce appetite and food consumption, they can also increase the risk of inadequate nutrition and loss of muscle mass. Over time, losing too much muscle can contribute to weakness, frailty, and other health complications.

Berkeley researchers wanted to investigate a fundamentally different strategy. Rather than focusing on reducing calorie intake, they explored whether it would be possible to increase the amount of energy the body burns.

This process, known as energy expenditure, includes the calories used to maintain basic bodily functions, regulate metabolism, and support everyday activities. Increasing energy expenditure could potentially help people lose weight without relying exclusively on eating less.

According to recent reports, "Body weight responds to two levers: taking in fewer calories, or spending more energy," mentioned Anders Näär, a professor of metabolic biology and nutrition at UC Berkeley and senior author of the study. "GLP-1s work almost entirely on the first, so we went after the second.".

A Compound That Burns Fat While Preserving Muscle.

The researchers focused on a molecule called 5-tetradecyloxy-2-furoic acid (TOFA), which has an unusual combination of effects on the body's metabolism.

Recent findings suggest that TOFA interferes with the production of lipids, a broad category of fatty substances that includes cholesterol and triglycerides. These molecules serve important functions, but excessive levels of certain lipids can contribute to metabolic disorders and cardiovascular disease.

At the same time, TOFA activates genes involved in taking up and burning fat for energy. This combination allows the compound to influence both how the body produces fat and how it uses fat as fuel.

In mice, treatment with TOFA produced several encouraging results. The animals became more sensitive to insulin, the hormone that helps move glucose from the bloodstream into cells. Improved insulin sensitivity makes it easier for the body to control blood sugar, an notable benefit for people with diabetes or insulin resistance.

The compound also lowered triglyceride levels and improved characteristics of fatty liver disease, a condition in which excess fat accumulates inside liver cells and can eventually interfere with liver function.

According to recent reports, perhaps most notably, obese mice treated with TOFA lost weight primarily through reductions in body fat, without experiencing significant losses of lean muscle mass. This distinction could be especially valuable because maintaining muscle is important for strength, mobility, and long-term metabolic health.

How TOFA Increases Energy Burning by 18%.

Although TOFA was originally discovered in the 1970s, the newly introduced research uncovered additional properties that could make it particularly useful for treating metabolic disease.

Sources indicate that the compound belongs to a group of substances known as ACC inhibitors. These compounds interfere with enzymes that help the body manufacture fatty acids, effectively slowing the production of certain fats.

According to recent reports, other ACC inhibitors have previously advanced to mid-stage clinical trials, but none has been approved to treat metabolic diseases. One major obstacle has been an unexpected side effect: many of these compounds increase triglycerides in the blood, potentially raising the risk of heart problems.

The Berkeley team discovered that TOFA does more than inhibit ACC. It also activates two cellular receptors called PPARα and PPARδ, which help regulate the genes responsible for fat metabolism.

It has been revealed that these receptors function as molecular switches. When activated, they stimulate processes that allow cells to absorb fatty acids and break them down to produce energy. In effect, TOFA simultaneously reduces the production of certain fats and encourages the body to burn fat that is already available.

According to recent reports, in mice, this activity increased energy expenditure by as much as 18%, without requiring additional physical activity or raising body temperature. Unlike other ACC inhibitors, TOFA also did not cause triglyceride levels to rise, potentially because of its additional effects on fat metabolism.

"TOFA appears to engage a coordinated metabolic response," said study first author Justin Y. Lee, a postdoctoral student at UCSF who conducted the research as a Ph.D. student at Berkeley. "It is not simply blocking lipid synthesis. It is also activating energy expenditure pathways that may help the body handle excess lipid and glucose more effectively.".

To understand whether these effects could be reproduced with separate treatments, the scientists gave mice a combination of two different compounds. One blocked lipid production, while the other stimulated energy expenditure.

Surprisingly, this two-compound approach was less effective at improving overall metabolic health than TOFA alone. The finding suggests that TOFA's ability to influence multiple metabolic processes through a single molecule may be an important part of its effectiveness.

Could TOFA Make Ozempic and Wegovy More Effective?

The researchers also investigated whether TOFA could improve the results of existing GLP-1 medications.

They tested the compound alongside semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, as well as tirzepatide, which is marketed as Mounjaro and Zepbound.

Industry observers note that these medications primarily help people lose weight by reducing appetite and food intake. TOFA, by contrast, targets the other side of the energy balance equation by increasing how much energy the body expends.

Sources indicate that when the researchers combined TOFA with these medications in mice, the results were more favorable than those produced by either treatment alone. The combinations led to greater improvements in body weight, blood glucose regulation, insulin levels, and triglycerides.

This suggests that treatments targeting calorie intake and energy expenditure could potentially work together to produce stronger metabolic benefits.

"In our combination experiments, TOFA worked additively or synergistically with the GLP-1 appetite-suppressing drugs, so we view it as complementary rather than as a replacement," Näär said.

In other words, the researchers do not necessarily envision TOFA replacing medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy. Instead, it could eventually become an additional treatment that helps address obesity and related metabolic conditions through a different biological mechanism.

A Promising Discovery, but Human Trials Are Still Needed.

Despite the encouraging results, the researchers emphasize that TOFA remains an experimental compound. All the findings so far come from animal studies, and scientists have not yet established whether it is safe or effective in humans.

Further research will be necessary to determine whether the same metabolic improvements can be achieved in people and whether the treatment could offer meaningful advantages over existing medications.

In a recent development, to help move the research toward potential clinical applications, the Berkeley scientists have established a biotechnology tech giant called ReRx Therapeutics. The effort has received support from the university's life sciences entrepreneurship network, including Nucleate and Berkeley SkyDeck.

If the findings eventually translate to humans, TOFA could represent an vital addition to the growing range of treatments for obesity and diabetes. By encouraging the body to use more energy while helping preserve muscle, the compound points toward a potentially different way to achieve healthier weight loss.

The research was funded through discretionary resources provided by UC Berkeley, with additional support from the UCSF Liver Center and the University of Michigan Animal Phenotyping Core.

Dang and Kook Son of Berkeley; Gracia Bonilla, Kashish Chetal and Ruslan I. Sadreyev of Massachusetts General Hospital; Kosuke Watari and Michael Karin of the University of California, San Diego; Christina Papa and Bilal N. Sheikh of the Helmholtz Center Munich; Prabha Ibrahim of ReRx Therapeutics.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alejandro Garnacho is yet to start a game for Aston Villa this season.

Alejandro Garnacho's time at Aston Villa has been brief - and it already looks to be over.

The latest snub by Villa boss Unai Emery was the most damming of all, with the on-loan Chelsea winger left out of Tuesday's Champions League defeat at Galatasaray.

"The players who were here I think are the best players to be here with us," mentioned Emery.

Villa could have had 12 substitutes in Istanbul but Emery chose just 11 - including two goalkeepers - as Garnacho stayed at home.

The plan was for the Argentina international's loan move to become permanent for Â£43m should certain criteria be met.

They are believed to be based on a number of appearances staff felt were so achievable the club were in little doubt he would become a Villa player.

But now there is doubt he will ever play for them again.

Garnacho trained with Villa's first team on Monday but did not travel to Istanbul.

"First start after three months. Happy to be enjoying football again.".

The post Garnacho wrote on social media after a pre-season game in July has - along with anything else related to Villa - been deleted from his account.

He has played just 34 minutes in the Premier League this season, and seven of Villa's 11 games ended without him getting on the pitch.

His last appearance - just a three-minute cameo - came in the 1-1 draw against Fulham on 31 October.

Including Saturday's 0-0 draw with Sunderland, Garnacho has been omitted from the past three matchday squads - a strong sign Emery has lost faith in him.

But he may have been fighting a losing battle from the off, having arrived at Villa unfit.

Sources have acknowledged the 22-year-old was not at the level required and were surprised how off the pace he was when he signed in July.

He initially trained on his own, and questions over the signing were already being asked, with eyebrows raised by some internally given his inconsistent form for both Chelsea and Manchester United.

Yet he had been on Villa's list of targets - albeit a long list - while he was at Stamford Bridge as Emery was keen to sign a pacy winger in the summer.

Garnacho's problems were compounded by a head injury suffered in Thailand in pre-season, and even a boot camp during the international break in September and October, and scoring in friendlies against Sevilla and Southampton have not helped.

One of the issues Villa have is there is no exit clause, and both teams would have to agree to end the season-long loan deal early.

This time last year, Emery had already decided not to sign Harvey Elliott permanently in a Â£30m deal, leaving the on-loan Liverpool midfielder in limbo for the rest of the season.

And it appears Emery has already come to the same conclusion with Garnacho.

Sources indicate that with Villa unable to find a solution with Liverpool, Elliott wasted a precious year of his career. Those close to him recognise the damage last season did, playing just nine times after being named Player of the Tournament at the European Under-21 Championship in 2025.

He is now at Valencia and is yet to start in La Liga this season.

It has been revealed that the risk of going on loan to Villa became a topic of conversation in the game because of Elliott's plight, with sources suggesting players would think twice about joining the club. Garnacho's situation only increases those concerns.

Three times in two seasons, Emery and Villa have signed a high-profile player on loan only for it to fail.

Jadon Sancho's expensive loan from Manchester United last season - Villa paying a guaranteed 80% of Sancho's wages of more than Â£200,000 a week - ended with him having made just nine Premier League starts and scoring once in 39 appearances, with 21 of those as a substitute.

Sancho may have played more than Elliott and Garnacho - and came off the bench in their Europa League final win - but what value did Villa really get?

Of course, Marcus Rashford and Marco Asensio enjoyed positive loan spells previously - Rashford returning to the England squad while at Villa - but they are exceptions to the rule.

Nicolo Zaniolo, Clement Lenglet and Axel Disasi have joined in recent years and barely merit footnotes, while Douglas Luiz's loan return last season did not prompt a return to the heights he had reached previously at Villa.

The club have constantly complained about financial restrictions with some justification, but questions can certainly be asked about the money spent on many of their signings.

The blunt truth is there is no clear path.

Teenager George Hemmings has just signed a newly introduced deal and has earned praise from Emery for understanding the way he wants his players to work.

Ibrahim Mbaye and Alysson are also ahead of Garnacho, leaving him well behind even before regulars John McGinn, Johan Manzambi and Emi Buendia are factored in.

There was interest from abroad in the summer, with Roma keen, and it seems increasingly unlikely we will see Garnacho at another Premier League club soon.

Fifa rules allow players to play for two clubs in a season - or three if they move to a team whose season overlaps like the MLS - meaning Garnacho could feature for another, unlike Elliott as he had already played for Liverpool and Villa.

Garnacho, whose character has not been called into question while at Villa, cost Chelsea Â£40m when he signed from Manchester United in 2025 but failed to make a consistent impression, with eight goals in 43 games. When he joined Chelsea he signed a contract until 2032.

Prior to that, United boss Ruben Amorim had told him to leave.

Now nothing, it seems, will persuade Emery that Garnacho is worth persevering with - leaving the winger's career continuing to drift.

Tech Report: Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1135 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the human family tree may be due for a major rewrite.
  • The study, published in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology, proposes a sweeping change to how we organize millions of years of human evolution.
  • Sources indicate that that would mean bringing groups such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus, which have traditionally been classified separately, into the same genus as modern humans.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the human family tree may be due for a major rewrite. Fresh research from Monash University challenges the traditional way scientists classify our ancient ancestors, suggesting that several groups long considered separate from humans may actually belong within our own genus, Homo.

The study, published in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology, proposes a sweeping change to how we organize millions of years of human evolution. Its central argument is that all human species and their closely related fossil relatives from the past 4 to 5 million years should be classified within the genus Homo.

Sources indicate that that would mean bringing groups such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus, which have traditionally been classified separately, into the same genus as modern humans. Although these ancient relatives differed considerably in appearance, anatomy, and behavior, the researchers argue that the evolutionary boundaries separating them are becoming increasingly difficult to justify.

Why the Human Family Tree May Need to Be Redrawn.

Human evolution is frequently illustrated as a relatively orderly progression, beginning with ancestors that resembled apes and gradually moving through species such as Australopithecus and early Homo before arriving at modern humans, Homo sapiens.

According to recent reports, however, evolution did not unfold as a simple sequence in which one species neatly replaced another. Instead, the fossil evidence reveals a complicated family tree with numerous branches, overlapping species, and evolutionary relationships that scientists are still working to understand.

Each new fossil discovery can complicate that picture. Traits once believed to distinguish one group of ancient human relatives from another have increasingly been found across multiple groups, making it harder to determine where traditional classifications should begin and end.

Dr. Ian Towle, a Research Fellow at the Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute and lead researcher on the study, argues that these discoveries are exposing weaknesses in the existing classification system. This applies not only to species already assigned to Homo, but also to members of Australopithecus and Paranthropus, groups that lived during the past 5 million years.

It has been revealed that "Recent fossil discoveries and advances in evolutionary and genetic analysis make this an ideal time to reconsider whether our traditional taxonomy still accurately reflects human evolution," Dr. Towle noted.

"These groups do not necessarily represent distinct evolutionary branches, or 'clades', and differences in behavior and ecology once used to distinguish them have also become increasingly difficult to maintain.

"I propose expanding Homo to include these other groups to provide a more accurate and stable way to represent the complex evolutionary relationships revealed by the growing fossil record.".

How Scientists Classify Our Ancient Ancestors.

To understand the proposed change, it helps to look at how scientists organize living and extinct organisms.

The system is known as taxonomy, which involves naming species and arranging them into groups based on their characteristics and evolutionary relationships.

A genus is one level of this system, sitting above the species level. Modern humans, for example, belong to the species Homo sapiens, with Homo identifying our genus and sapiens identifying our species.

Over the past 50 years, advances in evolutionary research have significantly changed how scientists approach classification. Rather than relying primarily on physical similarities, modern taxonomy increasingly seeks to organize species according to their actual evolutionary ancestry.

An important concept in this approach is the clade. A clade consists of a common ancestor and all of its descendants. By grouping organisms this way, scientists aim to produce classifications that accurately reflect the branches of the evolutionary tree.

According to recent reports, this approach has become increasingly influential in biology over recent decades. However, Towle argues that the classification of our own evolutionary relatives has been slower to adopt these principles consistently.

Why Brain Size and Tool Use No Longer Define Humans.

Traditionally, scientists have distinguished members of the genus Homo from other ancient human relatives using a combination of physical and behavioral characteristics.

These have included relatively large brains, sophisticated tool use, and particular anatomical features associated with human evolution.

But discoveries over recent decades have challenged the reliability of those distinctions.

Scientists have identified members of Homo with surprisingly small brains, demonstrating that a large brain was not necessarily a defining characteristic of every species in our genus.

At the same time, evidence suggests that species traditionally placed in Australopithecus and Paranthropus likely displayed more complex behaviors than researchers once assumed.

Industry observers note that together, these findings have weakened the boundaries used to separate the three groups. Characteristics once thought to be exclusive to Homo may have been shared more widely among our ancient relatives.

Sources indicate that as a result, determining which species belong within the human genus has become increasingly complicated. Towle argues that the problem may lie not with the fossil evidence, but with the classification system scientists are trying to fit it into.

A Radical Proposal for 5 Million Years of Human Evolution.

Towle's proposed solution is to expand the genus Homo to include species right now classified as Australopithecus and Paranthropus.

The idea is not that these ancient relatives were identical to modern humans or possessed all the traits associated with our species. Rather, the broader classification would recognize their evolutionary connections while still allowing scientists to distinguish among individual species.

Industry observers note that such a change could also make human taxonomy more stable. Instead of repeatedly revising the boundaries between major groups whenever newly introduced fossils are uncovered, scientists could use a broader genus that accommodates the diversity revealed by ongoing discoveries.

The proposal represents a significant departure from traditional classifications, and it remains a scientific argument rather than an officially adopted change. Nevertheless, it highlights how much our understanding of human origins has evolved as latest evidence has accumulated.

It has been revealed that "The more we learn about our ancestors and close fossil relatives, the more we realize how complex and non-linear our family tree is," Dr. Towle mentioned.

"Expanding the Homo genus to also include species of Australopithecus and Paranthropus will allow us to account for differences without regularly reclassifying particular groups.".

Ultimately, the research raises a fundamental question about how scientists define the human family. If the traits once used to separate our ancestors are not as distinctive as previously believed, the names and categories used to describe millions of years of human evolution may need to change along with our understanding of the past.

Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.
  • "This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.

"This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation. "People are displaced, people are dying of harm, hunger. It has implications on food security and livelihoods.".

In recent years, the East African nation has been hit by a series of climate-related disasters, from deadly landslides and floods washing away villages, to droughts damaging harvests and hydroelectricity production.

"When we come to COP and we talk of what the reality is on the ground, we Ugandans have suffered it," Anywar remarked, referring to the effects of climate change.

"It has an implication for the health of our people, on national budgets," she added.

Climate financing for developing countries to deal with the impacts of a warming planet has become a major sticking point at this year's climate talks. The gathering of some 200 states is seeking to close gaps on how to scale up financing from developed states and whether support should be provided through grants or loans.

Africa contributes less than 4% of the global greenhouse emissions that drive rising temperatures globally, but the continent is among the most vulnerable to climate impacts.

As it deals with the effects of climate change, including extreme weather, Uganda is also rapidly expanding investment in electricity production from renewables such as hydropower and solar.

In the country of some 53 million people, more than 90% of Ugandan households still rely on wood and charcoal as the most affordable fuel for things like cooking. Biomass accounts for 90% of the country's final energy consumption.

In a recent development, while using wood and charcoal leads to deforestation, Ugandans have little choice. Only around 2% of the country's energy comes from electricity — which is largely derived from hydropower — and less than half of the population has access to electricity.

"Now we are deliberately going into scaling up the production of electricity — hydropower electricity — and making it cheaper for cooking," Anywar stated. "We have other alternative energy sources... to mitigate this charcoal use. But the use needs to be phased out in a systematic manner by giving them alternatives.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

At the same time, the country is seeking to boost economic development by becoming an oil producer. Due to open in 2027, a controversial 1,443-kilometer (897-mile) pipeline is nearly complete. It connects two oil sites in eastern Uganda with a port on the Tanzanian coast.

Environmentalists have criticized the East African Crude Oil Pipeline project, which can transport up to 246,000 barrels per day. Environmentalists say it runs counter to the goal of limiting global temperature rise and could damage fragile ecosystems.

The Climate Accountability Institute said it would release 379 million tons of climate-heating pollution over its 20-year lifetime.

Oil wells for the project, operated by French energy giant TotalEnergies, are also located in Uganda's largest and oldest national park, Murchison Falls.

Industry observers note that "That has been also a sticky issue. And actually, that is one of the challenges we are facing at COPs," Anywar mentioned. She stressed that measures have been taken to limit emissions, and that the project was progressing in a "very deliberate way.".

The minister also urged developed countries to cut less wealthy nations some slack for using the resources they have to drive much-needed development, saying oil revenues could help fund the transition to cleaner energy.

Recent findings suggest that "You cannot tell us to cut off the umbilical cord that feeds us, as much as it has to be cut off," Anywar said, criticizing the lack of financing from developed countries to deal with climate change. "We are here begging for funds that are not forthcoming.".

Anywar added that developing countries "need a just transition," referring to an equitable shift away from fossil fuels that focuses on protecting workers and communities.

Another way Uganda is looking to finance climate change adaptation is through carbon credits, Anywar noted, describing them as a potential "breakthrough.".

Industry observers note that carbon credits are tradeable permits representing one ton of carbon dioxide that has been reduced or removed from the atmosphere through initiatives such as forest protection, renewable energy projects or tree planting schemes. Companies or governments can buy them to offset emissions they have not cut themselves.

"Our country is rich with biodiversity. And that is what we are looking forward to — attracting investors into our natural setup so that we earn some finances," Anywar said.

Carbon credits have been promoted as an key source of income for developing countries. But they have also faced criticism, for a lack of transparency and allowing polluting activities to continue.

According to recent reports, "We need to have a bankable approach to all interventions. Otherwise… it's not going to work for us," Anywar said, adding that her country also wants to attract investment and build partnerships in smart agriculture and the energy transition.

"If we rely on begging for funds which are not forthcoming, we shall go back empty handed.".

This interview also appeared as a video.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At the 2026 Billboard Latin Music Awards last month, a mob of Chuyíns in white straitjackets turned the stage into a psychiatric ward during a performance of “Pues Ya Ni Pedo.” The show’s closing gag revealed members of Fuerza Regida beneath the oversized masks — a fitting glimpse into the wonderfully chaotic world of the música mexicana breakout star’s May debut album, Los Locos Nunca Mueren (Crazy People Never Die).

But to understand the mysterious masked performer, first enter the void.

Industry observers note that “Before Chuyín, there was nothing, just black space,” the masked singer tells Billboard. According to his origin story, he came into existence on May 6, 2023, at a Fuerza Regida concert in Tepic, Nayarit, where frontman Jesús Ortiz Paz (JOP) “adopted” him. He’s been living with JOP ever since, he says, never once breaking character throughout the interview.

Industry observers note that chuyín is three years old — or 21, if you count in dog years, as he does — and already making his mark on música mexicana. His 16-track debut album, released May 7 via Street Mob Records, debuted at No. 9 on the Top Regional Mexican Albums chart and No. 17 on Top Latin Albums, both dated May 23. In September, “Pues Qué Le Hago?” gave him his first No. 1 on a Billboard chart, topping Regional Mexican Airplay.

Industry observers note that on Los Locos Nunca Mueren, which features Fuerza Regida, Calle 24, Luis R Conriquez, Óscar Maydon and Jorsshh, Chuyín takes on the carnal pleasures and intoxicating excesses common to contemporary corridos — then gives them a comedic twist. His protagonist doesn’t escape the consequences.

On “Paniki,” a cheating Chuyín goes to ridiculous lengths to conceal his infidelity, only to get caught when he tries his luck again. On the album opener, “Rehabilitado,” he declares himself rehabilitated while remaining tempted by his vices.

Sources indicate that “Everyone sings about the never-ending party. I sing about the hangover,” he says. “Everyone sings about partying, partying and partying. I sang about getting sent to rehab.”.

Consequences are central to Chuyín’s character, but so is perseverance. “Chuyín is the guy everything happens to, and somehow he gets back up and keeps going,” he explains. “Everything that could go wrong happens to Chuyín, and he gets up with the same smile and says, ‘OK, let’s keep going.’”.

Behind the irreverence is an emotionally invested songwriter. Chuyín says he wrote “Olvídate de Mí” entirely on his own while living through the failed relationship that inspired it. Rather than admit that he’s the problem, he tells his partner to forget him — and run if she knows what’s good for her.

Sources indicate that the song reflects the openness he says defines the album. “If you listen to my music, you know me, and you don’t need to know anything else,” he says. “I give myself to the public completely, emotionally. And I think that’s what connected with people.”.

In a recent development, for Chuyín, concealing his face affords him the freedom to bare his soul. “I feel like I’m mysterious, but I’m very vulnerable in my music,” he notes. “It’s a beautiful thing that people can get to know you without you showing your face, because of what you sing about. I always sing about personal things I’ve experienced.”.

Industry observers note that with JOP as his mentor, Chuyín has honed his songwriting chops alongside Street Mob’s wider circle of creatives. “For me, writing music is like therapy,” he states. His songwriting extends beyond his own repertoire: He also helped pen Fuerza Regida’s “Tu Sancho.”.

According to recent reports, onstage, Chuyín has experienced both the scale of a Fuerza stadium show and the intimacy of his own performance. Singing with the group at Mexico City’s Estadio GNP Seguros in front of an estimated 80,000 people was exhilarating, he notes. But a solo Chuyín show in Chicago, where 800 people had come specifically to see him, felt even more personal.

It has been revealed that “Both experiences were incredible, but they were very different,” he claims. “Every one of those 800 people came just to see Chuyín.”.

Sources indicate that name: Chuyín. Asked about the person behind the mask, he insists, “I’m Chuyín.”.

Age: 3 — or 21 in Chuyín years. Each year counts as seven because Chuyín is “like a little dog,” he says.

Born and raised: Tepic, Nayarit, Mexico; Rancho Cucamonga, Calif.

Recommended song: “Olvídate de Mí,” a candid account of romantic self-sabotage that Chuyín says he penned entirely on his own.

Musical influences: His personal Mount Rushmore of música mexicana consists of Alfredo Olivas, Gerardo Ortiz, Natanael Cano and Junior H.

Recent findings suggest that major accomplishment: Scoring his first Billboard No. 1 with “Pues Qué Le Hago?,” which topped Regional Mexican Airplay in September. “I put all the love in the world into the music,” he claims. “The fact that the public embraced it and that I made it onto the Billboard charts is crazy.”.

What’s next: Chuyín is working on his sophomore album and exclusively reveals to Billboard that he will embark on his first headlining tour in 2027, with further details to be revealed soon. The artist is preparing an immersive live show with one particularly mischievous tradition in mind: “At every show, I’m going to crown a Chuyín,” he notes. “With every show, there will be one more Chuyín in this world.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hanna Hattab has refereed in a number of competitions run by the Asian Football Confederation.

Claims that a referee was drunk during an Asian Football Confederation (AFC) Champions League Two match are "entirely unfounded", officials say.

Syrian referee Hanna Hattab was replaced at half-time of the match between Iran's Gol Gohar and Al Jazira of the United Arab Emirates.

Reports claimed Gol Gohar staff accused the referee of being drunk following what has been described as some erratic decision-making in the first half.

Iranian news agency ISNA quoted one club official as saying: "The referee was not in a normal state," and suggesting they would not have played on had the referee not been removed.

Accusations of drunkenness were also widely shared on social media.

But Hattab, who is part of the AFC's elite refereeing group, has released a statement denying the allegation, saying he has been defamed and threatening legal action.

The fourth official took over for the second half, with Al Jazira winning the match.

Hattab said he will be "issuing an official statement that clarifies all the details and facts related to what happened".

Omani sports journalist Issa Stated, who covers Asian competitions, claimed on social media that what happened to Hattab was "due to a drop in his blood sugar, which caused him to lose concentration and focus".

"He underwent a medical examination after the match and was not intoxicated, contrary to what has been circulating.".

In their statement on the match, which was played in Asia's second tier continental competition, the Syrian Football Association backed Hattab.

"Following an assessment of his health, it has been confirmed - contrary to various claims circulating on social media - that the reports regarding his situation are entirely unfounded," they wrote.

"The Committee reiterates its unwavering support for him and is committed to thoroughly investigating all details and circumstances surrounding the incident.".

#127910. Scientists turn Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks for future lunar bases

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (980 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists turn Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks for future lunar bases

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (980 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that building permanent bases on the Moon could become much easier if astronauts can turn the material beneath their feet into construction supplies.
  • Sources indicate that the study, published in NPJ Advanced Manufacturing, was led by first author Cole McCallum, who was an undergraduate student at the University of Arkansas when the research was conducted.
  • Recent findings suggest that to manufacture the bricks, the team used a 3D printing technique known as laser powder bed fusion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that building permanent bases on the Moon could become much easier if astronauts can turn the material beneath their feet into construction supplies. Researchers at the University of Arkansas have demonstrated a method for 3D printing simulated lunar dust into interlocking, LEGO-like bricks. The approach could eventually allow NASA to produce building materials directly on the Moon, reducing the amount of equipment and supplies that must be transported from Earth.

Sources indicate that the study, published in NPJ Advanced Manufacturing, was led by first author Cole McCallum, who was an undergraduate student at the University of Arkansas when the research was conducted. Wan Shou, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at the university, served as senior author.

Recent findings suggest that to manufacture the bricks, the team used a 3D printing technique known as laser powder bed fusion. The process begins by spreading a thin layer of powder across a flat surface. A concentrated light source heats the particles until they fuse together, a process called sintering. The printing platform then moves downward, allowing another layer of powder to be added and fused. Repeating these steps gradually produces a solid three-dimensional object.

Unlike Earth's soil, lunar regolith contains no organic material. Instead, it is made up of sharp, irregular fragments produced by billions of years of impacts from asteroids, micrometeorites, and other debris striking the Moon. Because actual lunar material is difficult to obtain, the researchers worked with a commercially available substitute called Lunar Highlands Regolith Simulant (LHS-1). This material is designed to resemble samples brought back by NASA's Apollo missions during the 1960s and early 1970s.

Turning Moon Dust Into Bricks Without Added Binders.

Industry observers note that previous efforts to 3D print structures from lunar regolith have relied on additional substances called binders to hold the particles together. Although these materials can improve the strength of printed objects, they introduce a major logistical challenge: the binders would need to be delivered from Earth.

According to recent reports, the University of Arkansas team demonstrated a different approach. Using a relatively low-power light source, they became the first researchers to directly fuse simulated lunar regolith into interlocking, reconfigurable construction blocks without adding a binding agent. Instead of relying on another material to hold the structure together, the lunar dust particles bond directly with one another.

"There's nothing else it's binding to. The regolith powder is binding to itself," McCallum said.

The team produced small bricks measuring a few centimeters across, including pieces shaped like crosses and the letter H. Their interlocking designs allow the blocks to fit together in a manner similar to LEGO pieces, potentially making it possible to assemble larger structures from individual printed components.

Sources indicate that however, the experimental bricks are not yet ready for demanding construction applications. Compared with objects manufactured using binders, the blocks made entirely from simulated lunar regolith contain more internal pores and have lower structural strength.

"These structures we're making can be self-supported," McCallum said. "But I would be hesitant to say our process could be used for something that's supporting other loads at this moment yet.".

Challenges Ahead for Building Lunar Bases.

Before this technology can be considered for actual construction on the Moon, several notable questions must be answered. Shou explained that scientists still need to determine how the printing process would behave under the Moon's low-gravity conditions and in a vacuum. The strength and durability of the finished bricks must also be improved to make them suitable for practical applications.

It has been revealed that despite these challenges, Shou believes the technique could eventually offer an efficient way to manufacture construction components and larger structures for permanent lunar settlements. The ability to produce interlocking bricks from locally available material could be especially valuable as NASA works toward establishing a sustained human presence on the Moon.

How Undergraduate Research Helped Drive the Discovery.

In a recent development, for McCallum, the lunar construction project was also an opportunity to gain valuable scientific experience early in his education. Originally from Little Rock, Arkansas, he joined Shou's laboratory during the early stages of his undergraduate studies at the University of Arkansas.

"He had this really strong belief that undergrads should get involved more with research," McCallum noted.

It has been revealed that mcCallum graduated in May with two degrees, one in mechanical engineering and another in physics. His academic achievements also earned him a place in the inaugural class of Lafayette Fellows, a competitive program that selected just 30 students from a pool of more than 3,400 applicants. Established to commemorate the 250th anniversary of the United States, the fellowship supports students pursuing master's degrees in France.

He is now studying aerospace engineering in Toulouse at the Institut Supérieur de l'Aéronautique et de l'Espace, also known as ISAE-SUPAERO, which ranks among France's leading aerospace engineering institutions.

Industry observers note that although his current studies have taken him in a different direction from the additive manufacturing research he conducted in Shou's laboratory, McCallum credits the experience with helping him develop essential research skills. Working through experimental difficulties and learning from unsuccessful attempts gave him a valuable foundation for future scientific work.

Sources indicate that "It helps you refine and overcome all the problems you have as a researcher. There are a lot of mistakes that I made the first time through," he said. "It was really nice to have a head start on everyone else and make those mistakes early.".

#127906. North Macedonia remains stalled on its EU path after 21 years as a candidate

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (853 w)

North Macedonia remains stalled on its EU path after 21 years as a candidate

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (853 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The European Union's enlargement drive has regained momentum: Montenegro could become the bloc's 28th member in 2028, while Albania is rapidly advancing through accession talks and could complete accession negotiations by the end of 2027 if it maintains its current pace of reforms.
  • But North Macedonia, an EU candidate since 2005, remains stalled on the road to accession.
  • That contrast will be particularly evident at Wednesday's EU-Western Balkans summit in Brussels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Union's enlargement drive has regained momentum: Montenegro could become the bloc's 28th member in 2028, while Albania is rapidly advancing through accession talks and could complete accession negotiations by the end of 2027 if it maintains its current pace of reforms.

But North Macedonia, an EU candidate since 2005, remains stalled on the road to accession.

That contrast will be particularly evident at Wednesday's EU-Western Balkans summit in Brussels.

It has been revealed that "The Western Balkans' future is in the European Union. Their accession is our priority, our shared ambition and a crucial geopolitical investment in these turbulent times," European Council President Antonio Costa mentioned ahead of the meeting.

North Macedonia formally opened accession talks with the EU in July 2022 but has yet to open the first of the EU's six negotiating clusters, the groups of policy areas through which candidates align their laws and institutions with EU standards.

But the lack of movement does not mean the country is unprepared for membership.

EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said in November that North Macedonia was "among the countries with the highest level of preparedness" in aligning with EU law and had recently accelerated reforms under the EU Growth Strategy.

However, she added, "the handbrake on its accession negotiations is still on.".

Kos said that to release this handbrake and open the first cluster, North Macedonia must adopt the constitutional amendment agreed with the EU in 2022.

For years, a dispute with Greece over the country's name blocked North Macedonia's progress along the EU accession path.

Although the 2018 Prespa Agreement resolved the dispute, and the country changed its constitutional name, clearing the way for NATO membership, a breakthrough on EU accession did not follow.

Bulgaria later blocked the process amid disputes over history, language and identity. A compromise brokered during the French EU presidency in 2022 lifted the veto but made further progress conditional on North Macedonia amending its constitution to explicitly include Bulgarians among the country's recognized communities.

The amendment requires a two-thirds majority in parliament, which has so far proved unattainable.

From the EU's perspective, this is no longer a Bulgarian veto, but a condition North Macedonia accepted as part of its negotiating framework.

In a recent development, "It [North Macedonia] is not blocked by a member state. It is blocked because it doesn't want to date to do what it knows needs to be done," Gert Jan Koopman, the European Commission's director-general for Neighbourhood and Enlargement Negotiations, recently told an Atlantic Council podcast.

North Macedonia's government sees the problem differently.

EU membership remains its declared strategic goal, but Skopje wants guarantees that amending its constitution will not simply pave the way for further demands from Sofia.

Those concerns are rooted partly in long-running disputes over identity and history: Bulgarian governments have challenged North Macedonia's interpretation of a centuries-old distinct Macedonian identity, while some Bulgarian politicians have gone further, describing Macedonian as a regional variant of Bulgarian, and Macedonians and Bulgarians as one people.

President Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova says North Macedonia is ready for talks with Bulgaria and the EU but wants certainty that one constitutional change will not simply be followed by demands for another.

"We only want certainty. We only want this not to be yet another amendment for the sake of an amendment, followed by another one," she mentioned.

After more than two decades of waiting, the deadlock has also become a domestic political problem in North Macedonia.

A nationally representative survey by the Institute for Democracy "Societas Civilis" illustrates the contradiction: 71% of respondents support EU membership, but only 24% back the constitutional amendments needed to advance the process. Among ethnic Macedonians, support for the amendments falls to just 11%.

Skopje-based political analyst Petar Arsovski describes the public mood as "passive-aggressive:" Strong support for joining the EU coexists with weak support for making the concession presently required to move forward.

That, he states, helps preserve the status quo.

The dispute is now deeply embedded in domestic politics in both North Macedonia and Bulgaria, where retreat from established positions could easily be portrayed as a national defeat.

The political cost is particularly high in Skopje, where the current government came to power in part on a platform of opposition to constitutional changes under the existing conditions.

For North Macedonia's government, accepting the amendments without further guarantees carries considerable domestic political risks.

The EU, meanwhile, is not offering to reopen the negotiating framework.

The uncertainty is compounded by debate over how future EU enlargement should work. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron have proposed allowing candidates to gradually gain some benefits of membership before formally joining, while stressing that full membership remains the ultimate goal.

According to Arsovski, uncertainty over the future course of enlargement gives ammunition to Eurosceptic narratives and reduces the political incentive for a difficult compromise.

"If these overall conditions remain unchanged, the most likely scenario is that EU summits come and go, while political actors remain dug in, with no real convergence of positions and no genuine commitment to a substantive compromise," Arsovski told DW.
