💡 Key Takeaways
  • FIFA have confirmed the hosts for the 2031 and 2035 Women's World Cup.
  • The United States, along with Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, made an uncontested bid to host in 2031.
  • In a recent development, FIFA's revenue for the 2026 men's World Cup was around $15 billion (€13.7 billion), and it's clear that US Soccer feels that hosting the women's tournament is the next move forward.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

FIFA have confirmed the hosts for the 2031 and 2035 Women's World Cup.

The United States, along with Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, made an uncontested bid to host in 2031. It will be the first tournament to feature 48 teams — as is the case with the men. The US has hosted the event twice before, in 2003 and 1999, and is also the most successful country in its history, having won it four times.

In a recent development, FIFA's revenue for the 2026 men's World Cup was around $15 billion (€13.7 billion), and it's clear that US Soccer feels that hosting the women's tournament is the next move forward. With the women's domestic league (NWSL) considered the strongest in the world and the US national team so dominant, securing the tournament in 2031 is a further sign of the US' committment to women's football.

"We expect and initiative for the 2031 Women’s World Cup to be the largest women’s sporting event in history," Emily Cosler, US Soccer’s vice-president of strategy told The Guardian.

According to recent reports, the 2035 tournament was also awarded to the sole bidders, England, Scotland, Northern Ireland and Wales. This sees the World Cup return to the United Kingdom for the first time since 1966, the only time England's men's team won the competition. The women lost the 2023 final to Spain. It also means that the UK will host two major tournaments in relatively quick succession, with the men's 2028 European Championships also set to be held in England, Scotland and Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the tournament would bring "visitors, investment and jobs to every part of the country.".

Given that FIFA President Gianni Infantino had revealed last year that both bids were unchallenged, this news comes as little surprise. Nevertheless, with the hosts now official, a 48-team tournament marks a remarkable advance for the women's game. The 2011 World Cup in Germany had just 16 teams.

In a recent development, the next World Cup will be in Brazil in 2027, running from June 24 to July 25. . Eighteen of the 32 teams have already secured qualification, including Germany.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The striking blue of the Betta Fish Nebula swims across the cosmic landscape, a stunning wisp of material leftover from a stellar explosion.

Roughly 6,800 light-years from Earth and nestled in the Centaurus constellation, this piece of the supernova remnant SNR G295.5+09.7 has earned the nickname the Betta Fish Nebula for its floaty, fishy shape.

Recent findings suggest that this almost ghostly whirl of gas and dust was created when a star much more massive than our sun exploded, blasting its outer layers of material outward in the process. Over time, the remnants of this supernova eruption stretched outward into space, dispersing and colliding with surrounding gas. The explosive remnants mixing with gas in the interstellar medium created this glowing, blue cloud.

It has been revealed that this celestial scene was captured by the Dark Energy Camera (DECam), that was created by the U.S. Department of Energy. The camera is installed on the National Science Foundation's Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in Chile.

This image of a colossal, cosmic "fish" was captured by a camera meant to study the illusive effects of dark energy, which is the name scientists have given for whatever mysterious something is causing the universe to expand at an accelerating rate.

The camera is used as part of the Dark Energy Survey, a six-year, international collaboration in which scientists have collected observations of hundreds of millions of galaxies, thousands of supernova and additional details about our cosmos that could help to fill in the picture of the nature of dark energy.

And while researchers this past January revealed the initial result of this six-year survey, scientists continue to explore the possibilities of dark energy with DECam alongside instruments like the recently-launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.

However, while the survey has lofty goals with its DECam data, the camera can also capture beautiful imagery like this cerulean wisp thousands of light-years away.

#127873. Latest Update: Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (870 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (870 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Medications you stopped taking years ago may still be influencing the bacteria living in your gut.
  • The gut microbiome is the vast community of bacteria and other microorganisms that inhabit the digestive tract.
  • Recent findings suggest that to investigate these connections, researchers examined stool samples and prescription histories from more than 2,500 participants in the Estonian Biobank's Estonian Microbiome cohort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Medications you stopped taking years ago may still be influencing the bacteria living in your gut. A large study from the University of Tartu Institute of Genomics has found that many commonly prescribed drugs leave lasting changes in the gut microbiome, even long after people stop using them.

The gut microbiome is the vast community of bacteria and other microorganisms that inhabit the digestive tract. These microbes play important roles in digestion, immune function, and overall health. While antibiotics are well known for disrupting gut bacteria, the newly introduced findings suggest that many other medications can also have effects that persist for years.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate these connections, researchers examined stool samples and prescription histories from more than 2,500 participants in the Estonian Biobank's Estonian Microbiome cohort. They discovered that most of the medications studied were associated with changes in gut bacteria. Even more surprisingly, a substantial number left detectable microbial "fingerprints" years after patients had stopped taking them.

Common Medications Leave Lasting Changes in Gut Bacteria.

It has been revealed that the findings extend far beyond antibiotics. Antidepressants, beta-blockers, proton pump inhibitors, and benzodiazepines were all linked to differences in the gut microbiome.

These medications are widely used to treat everyday health conditions. Beta-blockers are commonly prescribed for high blood pressure and certain heart conditions, while proton pump inhibitors reduce stomach acid and are frequently used to treat acid reflux. Benzodiazepines are often prescribed for anxiety, and antidepressants help manage depression and other mental health conditions.

It has been revealed that "Most microbiome studies only consider current medications, but our results show that past drug use can be just as important as it is a surprisingly strong factor in explaining individual microbiome differences," stated Dr. Oliver Aasmets, lead author.

This discovery suggests that looking only at the medications someone at the moment takes may overlook an crucial part of their gut health history. Previous prescriptions could help explain why the composition of gut bacteria differs so much from one person to another.

Anxiety Medications Show Effects Comparable to Antibiotics.

One of the most striking findings involved benzodiazepines, a class of medications commonly used to treat anxiety.

Researchers found that these drugs were associated with changes in the gut microbiome comparable to those seen with broad-spectrum antibiotics. These antibiotics target a wide variety of bacteria and are known to substantially alter the microbial communities living in the digestive system.

The researchers also discovered that medications within the same drug class did not necessarily produce the same effects. For example, diazepam and alprazolam are both benzodiazepines used to treat similar conditions, yet they appeared to differ in how strongly they disrupted gut bacteria.

This suggests that the effects of medication on the microbiome may depend not only on the type of drug being taken, but also on the specific medication.

Gut Bacteria Can Change When Medications Are Started or Stopped.

To investigate whether medications were actually contributing to these microbial changes, researchers collected additional stool samples from a smaller group of participants.

Recent findings suggest that by examining how the microbiome changed when people started or stopped certain medications, the team identified predictable shifts in gut bacteria. These findings provided additional evidence that the drugs themselves were contributing to the changes, rather than simply being associated with differences already present in patients.

Although the number of participants in this follow-up analysis was relatively small, the researchers were able to verify lasting effects associated with several drug categories. These included proton pump inhibitors, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and certain antibiotics, including combinations of penicillins and macrolides.

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, often called SSRIs, are a widely prescribed type of antidepressant. Macrolides are a class of antibiotics used to treat various bacterial infections.

Why Your Medication History May Matter More Than Previously Thought.

It has been revealed that the findings point to an crucial consideration for researchers studying the relationship between gut bacteria and disease. Differences in the microbiome may reflect not only a person's current health and medication use, but also treatments received years earlier.

If previous medications are not taken into account, scientists could mistakenly attribute certain microbial differences to a disease or another health factor when past drug exposure may have contributed.

It has been revealed that the results also highlight how much remains to be understood about the long-term relationship between medications and the gut microbiome. Although the study identified persistent microbial changes, these findings do not establish that such changes are necessarily harmful or that they lead to specific health problems.

"This is a comprehensive systematic evaluation of long-term medication effects on the microbiome using real-world medical health records," said Professor Elin Org, corresponding author. "We hope this encourages researchers and clinicians to factor in medication history when interpreting microbiome data.".

Weapons, war and wavering trust: Germans want to see more restraint in foreign policy

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (900 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For decades, German foreign policy was never seen as particularly controversial at home.
  • Long-held assumptions are beginning to crumble, including the belief that the US would ultimately remain firmly on Germany's side.
  • Recent findings suggest that in the foundation's latest poll on public attitudes on German foreign policy, 65% of respondents said they fear further military conflicts around the world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For decades, German foreign policy was never seen as particularly controversial at home. The country was firmly integrated into NATO and supported EU expansion and cooperation across Europe. It also advocated for multilateral approaches to resolving conflicts around the world. All of this enjoyed broad public support. But all of this has also changed since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the wars in the Middle East. Now, Germany's foreign policy has become increasingly contentious and is fueling growing public anxiety.

Long-held assumptions are beginning to crumble, including the belief that the US would ultimately remain firmly on Germany's side. This is one of the central findings of a newly introduced survey by the Hamburg-based Körber Foundation.

Recent findings suggest that in the foundation's latest poll on public attitudes on German foreign policy, 65% of respondents said they fear further military conflicts around the world. Meanwhile, 48% believe that Germany should adopt a more restrained approach to international affairs — a five percentage point increase from last year.

Since 2017, the non-profit Körber Foundation, established in the northern German city of Hamburg in 1959 by industrialist Kurt Körber, has conducted the annual surveys titled "the Berlin Pulse." For this year's study, the polling institute Forsa surveyed around 1,500 eligible voters in September.

It has been revealed that the findings make one thing clear: The current government's approach under Chancellor Friedrich Merz — seeking to have a say in virtually every international conflict and drawing on Germany's position as the largest EU economy — is increasingly met with skepticism. Only 40% of respondents now favor greater international engagement, down from 48% in 2025.

Florian Bigge, who helped compile the study for the Körber Foundation, commented on the findings on Monday: "This is a significant decline, especially since we have been asking this question for years, with changes in the range of just two to three percentage points.".

Meanwhile, 77% of respondents want Germany to focus primarily on diplomacy rather than military action.

According to recent reports, the most dramatic shift in public opinion concerns the war in Ukraine. Germany's military support for the Eastern European country, including the delivery of billions of euros' worth of weapons, no longer has the backing of a majority of the population. In September 2026, only 46% of respondents supported continued military assistance, compared to 59% in the previous year's survey. Right now, a narrow majority of 53% want to halt weapons deliveries altogether.

As Jonathan Lehrer of "the Berlin Pulse" explains, opposition is particularly strong among supporters of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).

In a recent development, "Eighty-eight precent of AfD supporters oppose military assistance to Ukraine," Lehrer stated. "This is an interesting finding, especially considering political developments in Germany, including state elections in which the AfD gained support by campaigning against aid to Ukraine.".

The AfD has recently overtaken the chancellor's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in nationwide polls.

It has been revealed that support for Ukraine was also the subject of a recent poll conducted by the opinion research institute Infratest Dimap. This study also found that public support for Ukraine is continuing to decline, with a majority now opposed to providing assistance (see graphic).

One finding from the Berlin Pulse study is particularly alarming for politicians and experts committed to transatlantic relations. As the US and China are increasingly seen as rivals on the global stage, 83% of respondents believe that Germany should remain neutral. Only 15% would side with the US.

Sources indicate that this may stem from the policies of US President Donald Trump. Florian Bigge of the Körber Foundation mentioned of the widespread preference for neutrality: "This sentiment is strong among Germans across all age groups and political parties. In eastern Germany, support for neutrality is at 92%, compared to 81% in the west. We interpret this as a desire for security but also reluctant commitment: Germans do not want to take sides in this conflict between the great powers.".

Recent findings suggest that the picture becomes clearer when respondents are asked about Russia. Under President Vladimir Putin, 82% of those surveyed see Russia as a military threat. However, public opinion is more divided when Germany responds firmly to such threats, including hybrid attacks. For instance, after the attempted drone attack on Leipzig Airport in early May, Germany responded by closing the Russian consulate in Bonn. However, only 51% support such measures, while 46% favor a more restrained approach.

"The gap between external expectations and domestic support is the central challenge facing German foreign policy," said Sarah Pagung of the Körber Foundation.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

One concern that appears to cause relatively little concern among Germans is the conflict in the Middle East, despite the devastating situation in the Gaza Strip following Hamas's terrorist attack on Israel more than three years ago.

Recent findings suggest that this may also have to do with changing public attitudes toward Israel. One question in the study asked: "Does Germany have a special historical and moral responsibility for Israel's security because of the Holocaust?".

The results were striking: 61% of respondents said no, while just 36% answered yes. Among those under 25, opposition to Germany's special responsibility toward the Jewish state was even higher, at 75%.

#127866. After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1607 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1607 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After eight years in space and a journey covering 10 billion kilometers, a pioneering X-ray telescope traveling to Mercury has captured its first observations of a distant cosmic object.
  • Industry observers note that scientists at the University of Leicester are now evaluating the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), which is traveling aboard the two-spacecraft mission.
  • The telescope has spent eight years traveling through space, making it essential to confirm that its delicate components are still working properly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After eight years in space and a journey covering 10 billion kilometers, a pioneering X-ray telescope traveling to Mercury has captured its first observations of a distant cosmic object. The instrument, built in the UK, successfully detected X-rays from the Crab Nebula, one of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky, marking an important milestone for the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's BepiColombo mission.

Industry observers note that scientists at the University of Leicester are now evaluating the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), which is traveling aboard the two-spacecraft mission. Their initial results are highly encouraging, arriving just as BepiColombo prepares to enter orbit around Mercury on November 21.

The telescope has spent eight years traveling through space, making it essential to confirm that its delicate components are still working properly. Although engineers monitored MIXS throughout the journey, the instrument could not look directly into space until September. That opportunity came after the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) separated from the two science orbiters, the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and Mercury Magnetosphere Orbiter (MMO) or Mio.

With its view finally unobstructed, MIXS could begin the critical tests needed before the spacecraft enters its planned orbit around the solar system's smallest planet.

A Telescope's First Look Across 6,500 Light-Years.

In a recent development, for its first astronomical target, the team selected the Crab Nebula, located approximately 6,500 light-years from Earth. This well-studied remnant of an exploded star produces a strong, predictable X-ray signal, making it an ideal reference for testing the telescope's performance.

By examining how MIXS observes this distant object, researchers can determine whether the instrument still performs as expected after its lengthy journey. They can also compare the results with laboratory measurements collected in 2015, when the telescope was last tested on Earth.

The main observation campaign took place on September 11 and 12. Over 39 hours, the spacecraft carried out 55 carefully controlled changes in orientation to collect the data.

In a recent development, one notable measurement was the telescope's angular resolution, which describes its ability to distinguish small details in an image. Scientists determined this by examining how widely the Crab Nebula's X-ray signal spread across the detector. Remarkably, MIXS delivered slightly sharper resolution than it had during its laboratory tests in 2015.

That improvement is particularly encouraging because the instrument will eventually use its X-ray vision to investigate the composition of Mercury's surface.

Better Than Expected After Eight Years in Space.

Professor Emma Bunce, Principal Investigator (PI) for MIXS and Director of the Institute for Space at the University of Leicester, welcomed the results as a major achievement for the international team responsible for developing the instrument.

Sources indicate that professor Bunce said: "We have waited a long time to make measurements with MIXS and it is fantastic to see it operating brilliantly in space. This is testament to our engineering and technical team, and our international partners who we have worked with over many years to build this incredible instrument. 80% of the technology on MIXS is newly introduced!

It has been revealed that "During our calibration observations we have determined that MIXS is generally performing fantastically well in space! We have no effects in our images that are associated with 'stray light' (optical photons getting in when they should not). We continue to see effects of galactic cosmic rays as we did during cruise, but we understand these and can filter them out. We see some self-fluorescence which appears when the Sun is illuminating the optic, but this won't affect our dayside observations of Mercury's surface. And the detector has suffered no radiation damage after 8 years in space.

"We see some effects in the instrument that we are still studying and expect to undertake some optimization procedures during the Mercury commissioning phase to fine tune MIXS in preparation for the science phase.".

The results suggest that the telescope has weathered its long exposure to the harsh space environment exceptionally well. Engineers have found no unwanted visible light interfering with its images, and the effects of high-energy cosmic rays are understood well enough to be removed during data processing.

The team has also identified a small amount of X-ray emission originating within the instrument itself when sunlight strikes its optics. However, this effect is not expected to interfere with observations of Mercury's sunlit surface. Most importantly, the detector reveals no signs of radiation damage after eight years in space.

Some remaining effects still require investigation, and scientists expect to make further adjustments after the spacecraft reaches Mercury to ensure that MIXS is ready for its full scientific mission.

How X-Rays Will Reveal Mercury's Hidden Chemistry.

BepiColombo is designed to investigate Mercury in unprecedented detail. As the smallest and one of the least explored rocky planets in our solar system, Mercury offers scientists a rare opportunity to understand how planets form and change under the extreme conditions found close to a star.

One of the mission's major goals is to uncover the planet's chemical composition and geological history. These findings could help explain Mercury's unusual characteristics while providing broader insights into the formation and evolution of the solar system.

Sources indicate that MIXS, carried aboard the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), will play a central role in this investigation. Developed by a European consortium led by the University of Leicester, it draws on the university's long history of X-ray astronomy research.

It is the first imaging X-ray telescope to operate on a planetary science mission. Working alongside other scientific instruments, MIXS will help produce a global map showing the elements that make up Mercury's surface, revealing its atomic composition in greater detail than ever before. It is also the only UK-led scientific instrument aboard BepiColombo and receives support from the UK Space Agency.

Sources indicate that the instrument works by detecting fluorescent X-rays released by rocks on Mercury's surface. When powerful X-rays from the Sun strike these rocks, they can cause atoms within the material to emit X-rays of their own. Different elements produce characteristic X-ray signals, allowing scientists to identify what the surface is made of without collecting physical samples.

MIXS will make these measurements with assistance from the Solar Intensity X-ray and particle Spectrometer (SIXS), which monitors the solar radiation and particles reaching Mercury.

The telescope will also examine X-rays emitted from Mercury's nighttime surface when charged particles associated with the planet's magnetic environment strike it. These measurements could reveal important connections between Mercury's surface and the surrounding space environment.

A 10 Billion Kilometer Journey With a Personal Legacy.

Recent findings suggest that for Dr. Adrian Martindale, MIXS Instrument Scientist at the University of Leicester's School of Physics and Astronomy, the successful observations represent the culmination of more than two decades of work.

Martindale joined the project in 2003 while still an undergraduate student and has been involved in nearly every aspect of the instrument's development.

Sources indicate that dr. Martindale stated: "BepiColombo, and MIXS in particular, are like part of my family. I've been involved since I was an undergraduate and touched almost every part of the instrument before it was rolled out.

Recent findings suggest that "This first data is mind-blowing to me. The last time we could see through this telescope it was in the basement under the School of Physics and Astronomy in Leicester, but after a rocket launch, eight years in space and 10 billion kilometers traveled it looks just the same. I can't wait to see the science data it produces when we get into orbit.".

The milestone also carries special meaning for the team because MIXS represents the scientific legacy of Professor George Fraser. Fraser was the instrument's original Principal Investigator and the driving force behind its innovative optical design before his death in March 2014.

Professor Bunce added: "We are thinking of George as we operate MIXS fully in space for the first time and know that he would be very, very proud of the team and delighted at our first light observations.".

BepiColombo Prepares for Its Final Arrival at Mercury.

BepiColombo began its arrival phase on September 3, when the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) separated from the spacecraft assembly.

In a recent development, the remaining connected spacecraft are scheduled to enter orbit around Mercury on November 21. The two science orbiters, MPO and Mio, are then expected to separate on December 9 to 10, allowing them to prepare for their respective scientific operations.

The mission's primary science phase is scheduled to begin in April 2027. Once underway, BepiColombo will investigate Mercury's surface, internal structure, magnetic field, and surrounding environment, helping scientists piece together the history of a planet that remains surprisingly mysterious despite its proximity to the Sun.

For the MIXS team, the successful first observations of the Crab Nebula offer an early indication of what the instrument may accomplish when it finally turns its attention to Mercury.

International Collaboration and Funding.

In a recent development, MIXS was developed through a partnership involving research institutions and technology companies across Europe. Participating organizations include:.

UK funding for the BepiColombo MIXS instrument comes from the UK Space Agency, which serves as the lead funding organization, along with STFC, the European Space Agency, and the University of Leicester.

#127864. What happens if a nuclear weapon explodes in space?

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (669 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

What happens if a nuclear weapon explodes in space?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (669 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A nuclear explosion in space would be unlikely to cause widespread injuries on Earth.
  • Sources indicate that in the United States, satellite failures could make it harder for emergency crews to communicate in remote areas.
  • We have some idea of what would happen because it's already been done.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A nuclear explosion in space would be unlikely to cause widespread injuries on Earth. But it could disable satellites that provide services we depend on every day, including some that save lives.

Sources indicate that in the United States, satellite failures could make it harder for emergency crews to communicate in remote areas. If GPS were also disrupted, drivers and pilots could lose navigation guidance, and financial networks could lose a source of precise time.

We have some idea of what would happen because it's already been done.

On the evening of July 8, 1962, people in Hawaii held "watch-the-bomb parties" and followed the countdown on shortwave radio. Then the night sky lit up. The United States had detonated a nuclear weapon about 400 kilometers (250 miles) above the Pacific. The test was called Starfish Prime.

Recent findings suggest that an electromagnetic pulse knocked out some streetlights in Hawaii, and some Pacific radio links briefly went down. The glow faded within minutes, but some satellites failed months later.

Recent findings suggest that the air was too thin for a conventional fireball to form or for a destructive shock wave to reach the ground. Charged particles made denser air below glow, creating an artificial aurora. The atmosphere also absorbed much of the initial radiation.

Satellites are especially vulnerable because they orbit above most of the atmosphere that shields people on the ground from the initial radiation.

In orbit, the initial burst of X-rays can damage spacecraft right away. But Earth's magnetic field can also trap electrons released after the blast, as it did after Starfish Prime. Satellites receive another dose each time they cross the resulting radiation belt. Over time, that exposure can damage electronics and solar panels.

That would depend on where the explosion happened and which satellites crossed the radiation belt. GPS satellites send signals that help phones, planes and ships work out where they are. They orbit about 20,200 kilometers above Earth and could keep working even if satellites closer to Earth failed.

Sources indicate that but satellites do different jobs. A ship's emergency beacon can use GPS to work out its location, then send it to rescuers through a separate satellite network. If part of that network failed, the alert could take longer to get through.

Recent findings suggest that the 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars its parties from placing nuclear weapons in orbit. The 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty prohibits its parties from carrying out nuclear explosions in space.

The Outer Space Treaty has no dedicated system for checking what spacecraft carry. A detonation is easier to detect because US satellite sensors are designed to pick up the signals it gives off.

Shielding could help protect satellite electronics, and backups could keep some services running. During a GPS outage, pilots over the contiguous US can use ground-based navigation aids. Operators could launch replacements, but those satellites could still face lingering radiation or debris.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Sources indicate that radiation could leave many satellites intact but unable to steer. If two objects collided, fragments from the crash could hit other satellites, creating more debris and triggering further collisions. If enough debris built up for the chain reaction to keep going on its own, it could continue even if no new satellites were rolled out. This is known as Kessler syndrome.

Recent findings suggest that whether an explosion would trigger such a cascade is uncertain. If it did, the debris could endanger replacement satellites for years.

Some radioactive particles could enter the atmosphere and eventually settle on the ground. But a blast in space is too far away to sweep up the soil and water that carry fallout from a surface explosion.

Industry observers note that as the particles disperse, their radioactivity decreases over time. The concentrated local fallout that can expose people near a ground-level blast to high doses would be unlikely.

FIFA has experienced a cyberattack, the football association first confirmed to Reuters and later Mashable.

On Thursday, the Fédération Internationale de Football Association said an external entity had accessed "a limited set of personal and ​business information" within the organisation. However, FIFA did not detail how many people or files were affected, or when it occurred.

"FIFA can confirm that it has been ​the victim of a criminal cyberattack resulting in ⁠unauthorised access to a limited set of personal and ​business information," a FIFA spokesperson told Mashable in a statement. "FIFA is working closely with the relevant authorities, including law enforcement.".

A group called the Handsome Boy Hacking Club has claimed responsibility for the cyberattack, according to the BBC, reportedly posting screenshots of FIFA documents online last week (the group has several posts on X declaring themselves the hackers). The news outlet said the group's claimed 12GB of accessed files amounts to less than one percent of FIFA's data. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that rocket Lab will add another satellite to a growing Japanese Earth-observation constellation today (Nov.
  • An Electron rocket carrying a radar imaging satellite for Tokyo-based Earth-observation organization Synspective is scheduled to lift off from Rocket Lab's Newly introduced Zealand launch site today, during a window that opens at 7:00 p.m.
  • According to recent reports, you can watch the mission, called "Night Owls Never Sleep," via Rocket Lab starting about 30 minutes before liftoff.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that rocket Lab will add another satellite to a growing Japanese Earth-observation constellation today (Nov. 26), and you can watch the action live.

An Electron rocket carrying a radar imaging satellite for Tokyo-based Earth-observation organization Synspective is scheduled to lift off from Rocket Lab's Newly introduced Zealand launch site today, during a window that opens at 7:00 p.m. ET (0000 GMT and 1:00 p.m. on Nov. 27 in New Zealand).

According to recent reports, you can watch the mission, called "Night Owls Never Sleep," via Rocket Lab starting about 30 minutes before liftoff. Space.com will carry the company's stream if, as expected, it's made available.

Synspective is building a network of "Strix" spacecraft equipped with synthetic aperture radar (SAR), which uses radio waves to generate detailed images of Earth's surface in both day and night lighting, as well as through cloud cover.

Industry observers note that today's launch will be Rocket Lab's 14th for Synspective to date, and there are a lot more coming. At the end of September, Rocket Lab unveiled a deal with the organization for an additional 20 Electron missions between 2028 and 2031 — the largest commercial launch contract in the rocket's history. That agreement brought Synspective's total number of contracted Electron flights to 47.

Synspective aims to eventually establish a constellation capable of imaging locations anywhere on Earth at intervals of just a few hours.

If all goes to plan today, the Electron's kick stage will deploy the Strix satellite into low Earth orbit, 569 kilometers (353.6 miles) above our planet.

"Night Owl Never Sleeps" will be the 101st mission to date for Rocket Lab. Ninety-two of them have been orbital flights with Electron; the other nine have been missions with HASTE, a suborbital variant of Electron that allows customers to test sensors and other equipment in the hypersonic flight environment.

Josh Dinner is Space.com's Spaceflight Staff Writer and a photographer with a passion for science and exploration. He has worked the space beat since 2016, covering the evolution of NASA's commercial spaceflight partnerships and crewed missions, planetary science missions, the Artemis program and humanity's return to the moon. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disney on Tuesday reported quarterly earnings and revenue that exceeded analysts' expectations and confirmed it's targeting $3 billion in cost savings by fiscal 2029.

Industry observers note that those cost-cutting efforts include several rounds of layoffs unveiled in recent months, Disney's chief financial officer, Hugh Johnston, told CNBC. The most recent round, which seeks to reduce costs by up to 20%, was reported earlier this month.

Future cost-saving measures will include reductions in administrative and other general expenses, Johnston said, while adding, "We do expect more layoffs.".

Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro told investors on the tech giant's earnings call that the job cuts are "not easy.".

It has been revealed that "They affect people who care deeply about Disney and have contributed so much to this manufacturer," he said. "At the same time, these steps are important if we want to be a company that moves faster, adapts to a rapidly changing environment, and keeps investing in the content and technology that will drive our growth.".

The cuts will help Disney fund its $26 billion in projected content spend for fiscal 2027, a 9% increase from fiscal 2026.

The entertainment giant is also forecasting double-digit growth in earnings per share in the next fiscal year, as well as segment operating income growth of around 8%.

Disney noted that the majority of that growth will be concentrated in the first half of the year due to the theatrical debut of "Avengers: Doomsday" and a boost from the Super Bowl, which will air on Disney's ESPN and ABC networks.

It has been revealed that "The growth is really going to come in the first half of this year," Johnston remarked. "That's the opposite of what we saw in '26, where the growth was backloaded.".

Recent findings suggest that the organization will also increase its annual dividend to $2 a share, a 33% increase from the previously declared dividend. It will be payable in two installments of $1 per share, one in January and one in July.

In a recent development, here's how Disney performed in its fiscal fourth quarter ended Oct. 3, compared with what Wall Street expected, according to LSEG:.

Disney reported net income for the fiscal fourth quarter of $2.61 billion, or $1.51 per share, compared with $1.31 billion, or 73 cents per share, during the same period the year prior.

Adjusting for one-time items, including severance and other restructuring charges as well as the value of intangible assets, Disney reported earnings per share of $1.77.

The manufacturer's revenue for the quarter was 16% higher year over year, and results were once again lifted by its parks and streaming divisions.

Recent findings suggest that disney's experiences segment, which includes its theme parks and cruises, reported nearly $10.11 billion in revenue, up 15% year over year. Operating income for the unit increased 20% to $2.25 billion.

The division is already a top performer for the company, but it benefited in the fiscal fourth quarter because of an extra calendar week compared with the previous fiscal year.

While international attendance continues to lag at Disney's domestic parks, it is being offset by domestic attendance, especially at the Walt Disney World resort in Orlando, Florida, Johnston said.

In a recent development, growth at Disneyland Paris was driven by recent investments including an expansion area called World of Frozen. Attendance at the Hong Kong and Shanghai parks remained soft because of broad economic challenges in those regions, according to Disney.

Still, D'Amaro noted he believes the growth in parks will be sustainable through next year, especially with new additions, including the "Monsters, Inc."-themed land "Monstropolis" opening at Walt Disney World in 2027.

In a recent development, "Q1 forward resort bookings at Walt Disney World are pacing up compared to the prior year," he said. "And latest capacity and new experiences will start coming online in 2027. We keep investing to make the experience fresh, and what we see is that drives repeat visits.".

Industry observers note that the manufacturer expects operating income for the experiences segment to grow in the high-single digits in fiscal 2027. Growth is expected to be front-loaded as the company laps the launch of the Disney Adventure cruise ship, which set sail in March.

According to recent reports, over at its entertainment division, Disney saw revenue increase 17% to $11.89 billion. Operating income nearly doubled to $1.33 billion.

Revenue from streaming, specifically, rose 19% to $6.1 billion, Disney mentioned.

The segment benefited from the extra week on the fiscal calendar as well as from growth in subscription and affiliate fees. Additionally, the organization saw higher theatrical distribution revenue from titles like "Toy Story 5.".

Disney said Tuesday it expects operating income for the entertainment division to grow in the high-single digits in the coming fiscal year.

Industry observers note that the company's sports division saw revenue increase 16% in the fiscal fourth quarter, reaching $4.61 billion. Operating income for the segment surged more than 50% to $1.39 billion.

Subscription and affiliate fees fueled this growth alongside an increase in advertising revenue.

It has been revealed that the company expects its sports division's operating income to grow by double digits in fiscal 2027. It noted that the fiscal first quarter of the year will see some declines because of the timing of College Football Playoff games and the New Year's window. However, the fiscal second quarter will benefit from the college championship as well as the broadcast of Super Bowl 61.

Disney's outlook for overall and segment results for fiscal 2027 excludes the impact of a 53rd week in fiscal 2026.

Sources indicate that D'Amaro has made advancing technology a pillar of the company's growth strategy. In September, Disney hired Karandeep Anand in the newly created position of chief technology officer.

"Technology is central to how we connect fans to more of Disney and drive returns on our investment," D'Amaro mentioned on the earnings call. "[Anand has] been energized by how much opportunity he sees to move faster and go further in product and technology. Done right, that means serving our fans even better, working more efficiently and being more innovative across every one of our businesses.".

Disney unveiled a partnership with Adobe earlier this month to develop generative artificial intelligence models.

D'Amaro told investors that the team is exploring ways to use AI to make booking trips to Disney parks easier.

Sources indicate that "There's actually a vacation planning tool that's in beta right now at Walt Disney World. We built that with our partners at Google, and I've had a chance to experiment with it myself," he remarked. "It'll be incredibly helpful for our guests who are booking trips. With these AI features, it can feel like you've got someone sitting right by your side, like a personal concierge, that prepares and responds to the way that you want to actually book your trip to Walt Disney World.".

The entertainment tech giant has also expanded its short-form content, adding a vertical video channel within the Disney+ mobile app. The company had previously announced a partnership with TikTok to bring creator content to the streaming app.

NASA’s Voyager 1 is now so far away that light takes 24 hours to reach it

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1641 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, NASA's Voyager 1 has achieved another extraordinary milestone, becoming the first spacecraft to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth.
  • The historic moment occurred on November 18 at 2:16 a.m.
  • The achievement marks another remarkable chapter for a probe that has traveled farther than any other human-made object, survived decades beyond its original mission, and continues to explore a region of space that no spacecraft had previously entered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, NASA's Voyager 1 has achieved another extraordinary milestone, becoming the first spacecraft to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth. After more than 49 years of traveling through space, humanity's most distant spacecraft is now approximately 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from home. At that distance, even a signal moving at the speed of light needs an entire day to make the journey.

The historic moment occurred on November 18 at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST). Scientists and engineers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, which is managed by Caltech, received a signal from Voyager 1 early Thursday, exactly 24 hours after the spacecraft reached the milestone.

The achievement marks another remarkable chapter for a probe that has traveled farther than any other human-made object, survived decades beyond its original mission, and continues to explore a region of space that no spacecraft had previously entered.

Voyager 1 Is Now 24 Light-Hours From Earth.

Astronomers often describe enormous cosmic distances in terms of how long light takes to travel them. A light-day represents the distance light covers in 24 hours, or roughly 16.1 billion miles.

Light moves through a vacuum at approximately 186,000 miles (299,000 kilometers) per second. To put Voyager 1's distance in perspective, sunlight passing Earth takes only about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon. Reaching Neptune takes roughly four hours, while traveling from Neptune to Voyager 1 requires another 20 hours.

According to recent reports, even these enormous distances are small compared with those separating stars. A single light-year, the distance light travels in one year, measures approximately 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers).

Voyager 1's extraordinary distance also creates a major challenge for mission controllers. Sending a command to the spacecraft now requires 24 hours, and receiving a response takes another 24 hours. A complete exchange therefore spans two full days, even though the signals travel at the fastest speed possible.

The milestone comes as engineers investigate a communication problem. NASA has not received scientific or engineering data from Voyager 1 since November 14. However, the probe continues transmitting a carrier signal, the radio signal that normally carries information back to Earth. By tracking this signal and calculating the spacecraft's trajectory, mission specialists were able to verify that Voyager 1 had crossed the one light-day mark. Engineers are continuing to investigate why the expected data is not coming through.

A Historic Journey Beyond the Solar System's Planets.

Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, were released in 1977 to take advantage of an unusual arrangement of the outer planets. The alignment allowed the spacecraft to use planetary gravity to travel from one destination to another, making an ambitious exploration mission possible.

It has been revealed that managed by JPL, the Voyagers became the third and fourth spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn. They also delivered the first high-resolution images of these distant planets, revealing extraordinary newly introduced details about their atmospheres, rings, and moons. Voyager 2 continued farther, becoming the first spacecraft to explore Uranus and Neptune up close.

Today, both probes are traveling through interstellar space, making them humanity's only spacecraft to have crossed into the region beyond the Sun's protective bubble. Their instruments continue monitoring changes in the Sun's magnetic field across immense distances, providing scientists with measurements that cannot be collected from Earth.

"Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler. The Voyager mission would be remarkable just for what it contributed to planetary science with the Grand Tour of the outer planets," said Joe Westlake, director, Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. "But it went on to become central to NASA's fleet of heliophysics missions offering insights into the star that we all revolve around, the Sun.".

Recent findings suggest that "Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery," stated Dave Gallagher, JPL director. "Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward fresh frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.".

Voyager's Golden Record Carries a Message From Earth.

Industry observers note that the Voyager spacecraft carry more than scientific instruments. Each also holds a Golden Record, a gold-plated copper phonograph record containing images and sounds representing life on Earth. These recordings were designed as messages that an advanced extraterrestrial civilization might discover someday.

The records give the mission a purpose extending far beyond its scientific discoveries. Even after the spacecraft eventually lose the ability to communicate with Earth, they will continue traveling through space with a small collection of sights and sounds from the planet that rolled out them.

"Nearly half a century after leaving Earth, the Voyager mission continues to push the boundaries of human exploration. Its epic journey reflects the vision of Ed Stone, the Caltech physicist and JPL director who guided the mission for decades, and the curiosity and tenacity of generations of scientists and engineers who have carried that vision forward," said Ray Jayawardhana, president, Caltech. "Beyond its immense contributions to science, Voyager also captures something profound about the human spirit. We may never know where its journey will ultimately lead, but it will venture on, an enduring affirmation that humanity was here and we yearned to explore.".

Exploring the Mysterious Region Beyond the Sun.

In a recent development, voyager 1 is right now moving through space at approximately 38,000 mph (61,155 kph). In 2012, it became the first spacecraft to cross the boundary of the heliosphere, a vast region surrounding the Sun that is filled with particles and magnetic fields generated by our star.

Industry observers note that this protective bubble helps shield the solar system from cosmic radiation arriving from elsewhere in the galaxy. Beyond its outer boundary lies interstellar space, where particles and magnetic fields from the broader galaxy become more dominant.

Voyager 2 followed a different route and crossed into interstellar space in 2018. Together, the probes are providing the first direct observations of conditions beyond the heliosphere.

In a recent development, one of their most intriguing discoveries is that the Sun's effects do not simply disappear at the boundary. Its influence appears to extend much farther into interstellar space than scientists once understood, raising latest questions about where the environment shaped by our star truly gives way to the surrounding galaxy.

"The Voyagers are revolutionizing our understanding of interstellar space, a previously unexplored region outside the heliosphere," stated Linda Spilker, Voyager project scientist at JPL. "One big surprise is the extent to which our Sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1. Where does the Sun's influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may endure long enough to answer that question.".

How NASA Is Keeping Voyager 1 Alive After Nearly 50 Years.

Operating spacecraft built nearly half a century ago requires increasingly inventive engineering. Both Voyagers have experienced problems as their equipment ages, including clogged thrusters and a malfunctioning computer. NASA engineers have repeatedly developed solutions that allow the probes to continue working despite these setbacks.

According to recent reports, electricity has become one of the mission's greatest limitations. Earlier in 2026, engineers took a calculated risk by switching off three devices aboard Voyager 1 and replacing them with three alternatives that consume less power. This change was intended to help the spacecraft stretch its remaining energy supply.

Industry observers note that voyager 1 depends on a radioisotope thermal generator that is now approximately 50 years old. Often described as a nuclear battery, the device produces electricity by converting heat released during the radioactive decay of plutonium.

As the radioactive material continues to decay, the available power gradually decreases. Both Voyager spacecraft lose approximately four watts of electrical output every year, forcing engineers to make difficult decisions about which systems can remain operational.

The latest conservation measures are expected to provide enough power to operate the spacecraft's current scientific instruments until at least the summer of 2027, when both probes will celebrate their 50th launch anniversaries.

One Day, Voyager 1 Will Become a Silent Messenger to the Stars.

Sources indicate that maintaining contact across such staggering distances requires some of NASA's most powerful communications equipment. The agency relies on its Deep Space Network, a worldwide system of large radio antennas located at three facilities, to communicate with Voyager and other spacecraft traveling to and beyond the Moon.

It has been revealed that despite the enormous communication delay and the spacecraft's aging systems, engineers continue monitoring Voyager 1 daily and transmitting instructions every week. The mission remains an extraordinary demonstration of what long-term spacecraft engineering can achieve.

"We listen to Voyager 1 every day and send commands to the spacecraft weekly. It just takes a little longer to communicate than it used to," mentioned Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL. "Even traveling at the speed of light, signals now take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft and 24 hours to reach us. One day in the future, when it can no longer communicate with Earth, Voyager 1 will become humanity's silent ambassador to the stars.".

#127855. Tech Report: German directors' doc on stolen film wins International Emmy Award

📅 24 Feb 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1047 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: German directors' doc on stolen film wins International Emmy Award

📅 24 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1047 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it sounds like the plot of a screenplay, but it happened to two Berlin film students in real life.
  • Moritz Henneberg and Julius Drost had created an animated short film for their final project at university.
  • "Butty" tells the tale of a household robot that gets kicked out when it can't do its job properly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it sounds like the plot of a screenplay, but it happened to two Berlin film students in real life. The documentary they made out of their unusual story, "The Talented Mr. F," has now won an International Emmy Award.

Moritz Henneberg and Julius Drost had created an animated short film for their final project at university.

"Butty" tells the tale of a household robot that gets kicked out when it can't do its job properly.

According to recent reports, when the two filmmakers posted the work on YouTube, this touching tale rapidly went viral. After generating a huge amount of hits, the duo decided to submit their work to festivals — but they were in for a shock: Organizers told them the film had already been submitted under a different name.

US student Samuel Felinton downloaded the film, made minimal edits, gave it a new title, "T-130," and removed the original credits. As the alleged author, he went on to win numerous prizes and made a name for himself in the United States.

Shocked by the blatant theft of their work, Henneberg and Drost sought legal advice. They were told that if they opted to sue, the process would be arduous and costly. So, the filmmakers took matters into their own hands and went to the US to confront Felinton — filming their journey along the way.

"We'd already made documentary films," Henneberg told DW. "And the idea just popped into our heads: This is a brilliant story — let's make a documentary about it.".

The two directors had developed a kind of fascination for the man who'd stolen their film.

Recent findings suggest that "We looked at his vlogs and sort of took a deep dive into his world," said Drost. "We almost saw him as a kind of celebrity. We discovered a lot about him and really wanted to meet him in person.".

While family and friends reacted with anger, the two young filmmakers remained surprisingly calm. They were more perplexed than anything: "Our families and friends hated Samuel. But we just wanted to understand what had happened," they said.

The pair put together a film crew and traveled to Morgantown, West Virginia — the university town where Felinton lives. With the help of a New York filmmaker pretending to make a documentary about young animators, they won Felinton's trust — and then Henneberg, Drost and Felinton were finally in a room together.

The two German filmmakers had prepared for all manner of scenarios ahead of the meeting: "We expected an emotional reaction — that he'd run away, cry, be ashamed or get aggressive. But he remained completely calm. That was the only thing we hadn't bargained for. We thought his world would implode. But he revealed barely any emotion at all," they recalled.

Industry observers note that felinton explained how he'd shortened and "improved" the film and that this was how it became such a success. He agreed to transfer any prize money. His manner was cool and matter-of-fact, which Drost and Henneberg found both unsettling and fascinating. After their chat, the three barbecued together and played a round of basketball.

Sources indicate that later, many viewers accused the two German filmmakers of being too soft on the plagiarist. Others praised their approach.

In a recent development, "The reactions were very divided," remarked Drost. "Some said we should've sued him or punched him in the face. Others said we'd shown newly introduced ways to resolve conflicts.".

"And in the end, it wasn't personal," added Henneberg. "He wanted to make something of himself — he could've taken another film. But if a big studio like Pixar had stolen our film, that'd be quite a different story.".

And so, Henneberg and Drost made the conscious decision to keep things respectful.

They didn't want to "publicly embarrass him or punish him any more than necessary," they said, adding that their documentary was sufficient "revenge.".

Industry observers note that the title of the documentary, "Der talentierte Mister F." ("The Talented Mister F."), is no coincidence. It's a play on the movie title "The Talented Mr. Ripley," the story of a young man who assumes the identity of a wealthy heir and ends up mired in a web of lies, fraud and, finally, murder. And just like Mr. Ripley, Felinton had also assumed a false identity.

Felinton did actually end up sending them the trophies he had won, as well as a sum of money.

For their part, however, the festivals preferred to keep their distance from the saga. As one organizer said: The prize has been awarded, and there's nothing we can do about it — it's up to these guys to work things out between themselves.

Industry observers note that for the original filmmakers themselves, the scandal has also had a positive impact: Since the documentary was released in Germany in October 2025, their animation film has garnered even more attention on YouTube. Henneberg and Drost uploaded it again, and in the credits, special thanks also go out to Samuel Felinton.

And now, the documentary is winning its own awards: Before being honored with the International Emmy Award, it also won a Grimme Prize, one of Germany's most prestigious television awards.

Felinton was able to steal the film in the first place in part because when it first appeared online in 2023, it could just be downloaded from YouTube.

Drost and Henneberg say uploading "Butty" back then wasn't a mistake, saying that was the risk of putting something online.

The alternative would have been not to show the film at all, they mentioned; then no one would have seen it.

They have a clear message for young creatives.

Sources indicate that "Don't be discouraged. Be aware that something like this can happen — but stay creative in how you deal with it. Suing is expensive and often doesn't do much good. Instead, show the world that you're the authors.".

Recent findings suggest that what started out as film plagiarism ended up becoming material for another project. And that's perhaps the most unusual twist in this very quirky story.

This article was originally published in German in February 2026 and was updated on November 24, 2026, following the International Emmy Awards.

Tech Report: A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1827 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronomers have uncovered an extraordinary stellar collision in the neighboring Andromeda galaxy, where a smaller star spiraled into a gigantic supergiant and ultimately merged with it.
  • It has been revealed that researchers have nicknamed the resulting star Bao, describing it as potentially "rejuvenated" by the merger.
  • Industry observers note that observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope provided crucial evidence of what happened.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronomers have uncovered an extraordinary stellar collision in the neighboring Andromeda galaxy, where a smaller star spiraled into a gigantic supergiant and ultimately merged with it. The rare event, the first of its kind to be identified, left behind a single star that may have been given a new lease on life.

It has been revealed that researchers have nicknamed the resulting star Bao, describing it as potentially "rejuvenated" by the merger. The smaller star was slightly less massive than our Sun, while its enormous companion was a swollen supergiant. The dramatic encounter took place near the outer edge of Andromeda and was investigated through a NASA-funded research effort.

Industry observers note that observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope provided crucial evidence of what happened. By combining Webb's findings with years of measurements from ground-based and space telescopes, scientists were able to reconstruct the stars' remarkable transformation.

It has been revealed that "Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict," said Viraj Karambelkar, the first author of a latest paper in Nature and a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York. "However, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the stars' eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescope's data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing.".

How a Giant Star Swallowed Its Companion.

In a recent development, for thousands of years, the two stars existed as a binary system, orbiting one another without merging. That long period of relative stability ended when the smaller star began brushing against the enormous outer atmosphere of its companion.

Once that interaction started, the process moved surprisingly quickly. The two stars completed their "unification" after just seven additional orbits (about seven years). Previously observed mergers involving pairs of smaller stars had required thousands of orbits to reach the same outcome.

The speed of the final eruption also caught astronomers off guard.

"We thought an outburst from such an extended star would take years," noted co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. "One day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!".

Scientists had already detected subtle warning signs before the eruption. As the smaller star moved through the giant's outer atmosphere, it disturbed the surrounding gas and began stripping away material, gradually changing the system's brightness.

"When a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect -- a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Bao's data," stated co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in New York. "As the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary star's outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space.".

A Violent Stellar Merger With More Than One Possible Outcome.

It has been revealed that this kind of interaction is part of a process astronomers call common envelope evolution. It occurs when two stars become surrounded by a shared outer layer of gas, typically after one star expands enough to engulf its companion.

As the smaller star moves through that gas, resistance slows its orbit and drains away orbital energy. The companion can then spiral progressively deeper toward the center of the larger star.

For Bao, the smaller star ultimately plunged inward and merged with the giant. Webb's observations provided the evidence needed to confirm that the stars had become one.

Sources indicate that but such encounters do not always end with a merger. Sometimes, both stars survive, losing substantial amounts of material while emerging as two separate objects locked in much tighter orbits.

It has been revealed that these surviving systems are vital because they can eventually produce some of the universe's most extreme phenomena. Depending on how the stars evolve, they may become neutron stars or black holes, undergo violent supernovae, generate gravitational waves that ripple through space-time, or form rapidly rotating objects called millisecond pulsars.

Understanding common envelope evolution is therefore essential to explaining how many of these extraordinary cosmic objects come into existence.

Reconstructing the Collision With James Webb.

To understand exactly what happened to Bao, the researchers refined computer simulations of the two stars and compared the results with Webb's observations.

The telescope's mid-infrared measurements were particularly valuable because they revealed dust that the giant star had expelled over hundreds of years. Infrared light allows astronomers to study material that can be difficult to detect at visible wavelengths, offering clues about the system's history long before its final eruption.

Recent findings suggest that the simulations revealed that the larger star had been truly enormous. Before the merger, it was approximately seven times as massive as the Sun, had a radius 350 times larger, and shone with 18,000 times the Sun's brightness.

Those staggering proportions earned it the nickname "Big Bao.".

Recent findings suggest that "It was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data," remarked co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations.

Industry observers note that the researchers also calculated the mass of the smaller star for the first time. Nicknamed "Little Bao," it was likely somewhat smaller and dimmer than the Sun, with an estimated mass of (about 0.7 solar masses). In other words, it contained roughly 70% as much mass as our star.

At first, the simulations suggested that the smaller companion might have retained enough energy to "flee" the giant's gravitational grip and escape the encounter.

Further investigation, however, revealed a very different ending. Little Bao had been dragged deep into the core of Big Bao, releasing an immense amount of energy as the two stars merged.

Their final encounter was "almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star," De remarked.

The merger has left astronomers with another key question: What is Bao like now?

The surviving star contains the legacy of both original stars, but its final structure and mass distribution remain uncertain. Future observations will be needed to determine how its "heft" settles as the newly merged object evolves.

Years of Telescope Observations Reveal the Warning Signs.

One reason this discovery is so valuable is that scientists had been watching Bao long before its dramatic eruption.

Although Webb supplied crucial information about the amount of material expelled and how efficiently the common envelope process unfolded, the team also drew on ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared observations from multiple observatories. Together, these measurements provided a detailed record of the system's changing behavior as the merger approached and unfolded.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers had even published an earlier study shortly before the stars erupted. (In fact, they published their first paper right before the eruption in 2025.).

The first major clue appeared in February 2023, when astronomers examining archived observations from NASA's retired NEOWISE (Near-Earth Object Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer) mission noticed a star whose brightness was behaving unusually.

Earlier records revealed that the object had maintained a steady luminosity before 2018. Its later variations suggested that something significant was beginning to change.

Sources indicate that by September 2024, observations from the Wide-field Infrared Transient Explorer (WINTER) indicated further evidence of activity. The system was growing brighter and releasing dust into the surrounding space.

Another important development came in July 2025, when NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) happened to observe Bao during a routine sky survey.

In a recent development, the telescope detected a striking change: Bao was rapidly fading in visible light while simultaneously becoming brighter in infrared light. This unusual combination provided another sign that the system was undergoing a major transformation.

Industry observers note that then, on October 17, 2025, the Zwicky Transient Facility detected the eruption. The observations revealed a sudden surge in brightness accompanied by a dramatic increase in temperature.

Scientists promptly arranged additional observations to capture the unfolding event. In November 2025, NASA's now-retired Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory and NOIRLab's Gemini North telescope in Hawaii supplied valuable new measurements.

In a recent development, webb joined the effort on December 24, 2025, through an urgently approved Director's Discretionary Time program. This special observing opportunity allowed the telescope to examine the aftermath while the system was still undergoing rapid changes.

A New Window Into the Lives and Deaths of Stars.

The successful investigation of Bao, officially designated AT 2025abao, represents an key advance in the study of stellar mergers.

Rather than trying to reconstruct a cosmic event that occurred hundreds, thousands, or even millions of years earlier, astronomers were able to observe and analyze the process as it happened.

It has been revealed that that timing made it possible to measure how efficiently the common envelope interaction transferred energy and expelled material from the system. Such measurements can help researchers improve their models of how binary stars evolve and what determines whether they merge or survive.

The discovery also arrives at an especially promising time for astronomy.

NASA's recently released Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is preparing to carry out extensive publicly available surveys that could reveal many more unusual stellar events.

Industry observers note that one of its major observing programs, the Galactic Bulge Time-Domain Survey, will repeatedly monitor large numbers of stars, helping astronomers identify objects whose brightness or appearance changes over time. These temporary or changing phenomena, known as transient events, may include additional systems undergoing transformations similar to Bao's.

With more discoveries and coordinated follow-up observations, researchers could gain a much clearer understanding of how often stars engulf their companions and what happens afterward.

"There's going to be a large influx of similar discoveries just ahead," Karambelkar remarked.

The research received partial funding through NASA's Astrophysics Data Analysis Program.

Recent findings suggest that the James Webb Space Telescope, the largest and most powerful space observatory ever launched, supports the work of thousands of astronomers around the world. Its scientific mission includes investigating objects within our solar system, exploring planets orbiting distant stars, and studying the formation, structure, and evolution of the universe to better understand our cosmic origins and place within it.

Webb is an international collaboration led by NASA in partnership with ESA (European Space Agency) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Home Depot on Tuesday declared its chief financial officer, Richard McPhail, will become CEO of the organization, succeeding Ted Decker, effective next week.

Recent findings suggest that alongside McPhail's appointment, Home Depot said Ann-Marie Campbell, currently senior executive vice president of U.S. stores and operations, will become president and chief operating officer. Jordan Broggi has been chosen as CFO to succeed McPhail.

According to recent reports, decker, CEO since 2022, had been on temporary medical leave since August. The firm said on Tuesday that Decker has returned from leave but is now stepping down from his role. He will continue to serve as chair of the board of directors, the company said.

"I'm glad to be back and grateful for the support I received," Decker told analysts on Tuesday. "The board and I have agreed that now is the right time to move to the next phase of our succession plan.".

McPhail has been with the manufacturer since 2005, holding multiple executive roles.

"We're not going to change course," McPhail told CNBC's Becky Quick.

He remarked the manufacturer will continue to lean into winning professional shoppers like contractors and using artificial intelligence tools to encourage sales. McPhail added that while the company faces more challenges now than it did at the start of the year, it is still winning share of the home improvement market.

Industry observers note that home Depot has been pressured by a sluggish housing market, higher mortgage rates and a more cautious consumer. Still, the company has previously said it's seen resilience among its pro shoppers who are still shopping for their home improvement projects.

Shares of Home Depot sank more than 3% following the announcement and the retailer's fiscal third-quarter results.

The CEO change came as the home improvement retailer posted quarterly earnings and revenue that beat analysts' expectations. The tech giant noted comparable sales rose 2.2% during the period, compared with estimates of up 1.8%, according to StreetAccount.

Here's how Home Depot performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

The company reported net income of $3.71 billion, or $3.72 per share, compared with $3.60 billion, or $3.62 per share, the year prior. Excluding one-time items, Home Depot reported adjusted earnings per share of $3.86.

Revenue rose 4.9% compared with the year-ago period.

"We also are confident that we are taking material share from the market and from competition," McPhail remarked on the call with analysts.

In the third quarter, the manufacturer mentioned online comparable sales grew around 13%, which marked its sixth straight quarter of double-digit positive growth for the metric.

The tech giant remarked it saw positive comparable sales numbers in 13 out of 16 of its merchandising departments, including notable strength in the power department, which posted double-digit percentage growth.

Industry observers note that for the full year, Home Depot stated it expects total sales to rise roughly 4.5%, the top end of its previously provided range. It also anticipates comparable sales will grow around 1.4%, compared with an outlook of flat to a 2% increase.

Home Depot added it expects adjusted earnings per share to rise 2% this year, compared with prior guidance of flat to a 4% increase.
